Calhoun barely pitched as a Mississippi freshman and handled a middle-relief role as a sophomore before getting trusted with higher-leverage situations on a Men's College World Series team this spring. Though he has made just two starts in three college seasons, some evaluators are intrigued by the idea of moving him to the rotation in pro ball. His baseball lineage extends further back than most, as his great-grandfather Chick Green played for the Rebels in 1914 under coach Casey Stengel, who went on to become a Hall of Famer as a big league manager. Calhoun's fastball usually ranges from 93-95 mph and maxes out at 97, missing a lot of bats with explosive carry and some armside run. He uses five different pitches, and his best secondary options are an upper-80s cutter and a low-80s slider with depth. His upper-80s changeup and his upper-70s curveball play as average offerings. There's a bit of effort in Calhoun's up-tempo delivery that hampers his ability to locate his pitches where he wants. He has improved his strike throwing during his time in Oxford, but he still has below-average control and fastball command. He has five viable pitches and some projection still remaining in his 6-foot-4 frame, so he'll have no shortage of suitors.

Sdao featured the best arsenal on Texas A&M's 2024 College World Series runner-up club, but injured his elbow in the Super Regionals and had Tommy John surgery that fall. He missed the entire 2025 season, but still drew seven-figure bonus offers from several big league teams before deciding to return to the Aggies. His stuff and command haven't been as sharp as they were during his freshman season, but he still offers enough upside to go in the top three rounds. Before his elbow gave out, Sdao operated with a 92-94 mph fastball that touched 97 with good carry up in the zone. This spring, his velocity has been down a tick or two and his release point has risen a few inches, so he's not missing as many bats with his heater. His best pitch is a sweeping low-80s slider that can overmatch both lefty and righty hitters, though it hasn't been as dominant in 2026. He has added a mid-70s curveball and a mid-80s cutter that both grade around average, surpassing his sinking mid-80s changeup that has regressed. Sdao has a wiry 6-foot-3 frame with room to add strength, and he generates his stuff with arm speed rather than effort. He throws strikes with all of his pitches and has demonstrated plus fastball command in the past. Now a redshirt junior, he offers intrigue as a mid-rotation lefty starter if he regains his previous fastball and slider.

Durnin spent two years at Wichita State and won the Appalachian League Player of the Year award last summer before transferring to Missouri, where he led the Tigers in all three slash stats (.329/.438/.507). He has 15-homer potential, average speed and a chance to stick at shortstop in pro ball.

Like his older brother Connor before him, Ethan Norby is an undersized star at East Carolina who draws rave reviews for his competitiveness. While Connor was a sweet-swinging infielder who went to the Orioles in 2021's second round en route to the big leagues, Ethan is a left-hander with one of the better sliders in college baseball. He didn't quite live up to expectations this spring but still could factor into the top three or four rounds. Norby's high-spin 79-82 mph slider features plenty of sweep and depth, and it was outstanding when he struck out a Pirates-record 19 against eventual College World Series runner-up Coastal Carolina last March, though it can get roughed up when it catches too much of the plate. He's throwing a tick harder this year, parking at 91-92 mph and topping out at 95 with his fastball, but it isn't missing as many bats with its carry as it has in the past. He's struggling to land his tumbling mid-80s changeup for strikes, while his mid-80s cutter lags behind the rest of his repertoire. The 5-foot-10 Norby leans into his lack of size by getting down the mound and using a three-quarters arm slot to create a low release height and good shape on his pitches. His slingy delivery and short arm action add to his deception without compromising his control or fastball command, though he hasn't been quite as sharp as he was as a sophomore. He profiles best as a slider-happy reliever but his aptitude and makeup could make him a back-of-the-rotation starter.

Lewis broke into college baseball by winning the Big East Conference batting title (.377) and freshman of the year award in 2024. He transferred to Wake Forest last year and has posted similar numbers against better competition, while also earning All-Star honors in the Cape Cod League. His hitting ability is unquestioned, but how much a club believes he can offer beyond that will determine how high he climbs in the Draft. Lewis employs a simple setup and a flat left-handed swing geared for contact. He controls the barrel very well, focusing on lacing line drives from gap to gap, and he destroys fastballs perhaps better than any hitter in college baseball. While he's 6-foot-2 and 220 pounds, he may not have more than average bat speed or raw power, though his bat-to-ball skills should help him get to most of it. If Lewis winds up at first base, which is where Wake Forest plans to deploy him this season, his relative lack of pop may become an issue. He played mostly third base in 2025, but he's an erratic defender with just average arm strength there. He's a fringy athlete and could get a look in left field after he turns pro.

Hailing from Oakton High School in Virginia, Lavey stayed in the region to head to George Washington University to extend his baseball career. He made an immediate impact as a freshman, earning second-team All Atlantic 10 honors, repeating the feat again as a junior. In between, he was a Cape Cod League All-Star. His solid showing on the Cape, carrying that over to the 2026 season and constant need for decent all-around catchers had teams considering Lavey in the top several rounds. Lavey checks off an oft-coveted box as a left-handed-hitting catcher. Nothing he does is flashy, but he can do everything pretty well. He has an easy swing, with a line-drive, up the middle approach, and he has the strength to drive the ball at times, with solid exit velocity data to back that up. He doesn't swing and miss or chase much and walked more than he struck out as a junior. Behind the plate, there's work to be done, but he has the makings of a solid defensive backstop, one with an above-average arm and pop times under 2.00 seconds. He'd receive better instruction on his glove work on the pro side, so there's some ceiling to reach there. That and his steady bat had some believing he could go in the top five rounds come Draft time.

Contreras spent a year at Modesto Junior College before moving on to Cal State Fullerton. He was named Big West Co-Player of the Year as a junior in 2026 following a .346/.441/.633 line to go along with 14 homers. He’s a big, physical right-handed hitter who made some subtle changes at the plate to unlock some of his tools as a junior. Still only 20, he’s played right field mostly in college, but some scouts think he should get a look in center as a pro.

Sheerin broke into college baseball by winning Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference Rookie of the Year accolades and setting Mount St. Mary's records for strikeouts (109), strikeouts per nine innings (14.0) and opponent average (.197) in 2024. One of the top transfers on the portal market that year, he moved to Louisiana State but tore an anterior cruciate ligament while playing basketball that summer and missed all of 2025 following left knee surgery. He has returned this year throwing 3 mph harder than he did as a freshman and some teams rate him as the best reliever available. Sheerin's fastball now sits at 95-97 mph and tops out at 100, exploding on hitters with carry and armside run. He does a nice job of throwing his tight mid-80s slider for strikes, though it doesn't miss as many bats as it should. He'll flash a low-80s curveball with depth and an upper-80s splitter, but he relies almost exclusively on his heater and slide piece. Sheerin has a 6-foot-5 frame and gets down the mound well, creating good extension, and his low arm slot and crossfire delivery provide plenty of deception. With his mechanics and effort, he's definitely a reliever. If he can upgrade his slider and fringy control, he could be a late-inning option as a pro.

St. John Bosco High School in California has been a nationally ranked team this spring, with a talented roster typically led by infielder James Clark. Scouts could often double up on days that Garcia was pitching, and there have been times this year that the 6-foot-3 right-hander has stolen the headlines. Garcia has excelled under the spotlight, landing in the top five in average velocity and average breaking ball spin rate in his start at USA Baseball's National High School Invitational, then outpitching Orange Lutheran's Gary Morse back home in California. At his best, Garcia can show off two plus pitches in his fastball and curve. While he'll pitch anywhere in the 92-97 mph range, he's answered questions about maintaining his stuff by carrying mid-90s heat deep into starts, and there could be even more consistent velocity down the road. He throws it with 18-19 inches of ride, a four-seamer with true carry. He backs it up with a nasty 12-to-6 curve that has been known to register 3,000 rpm spin rates. He has a changeup and has shown some feel for it, but he doesn't need it given how good the fastball-curve combination is. Making Garcia's current two-pitch mix play up is his ability to throw it consistently for strikes. He often commands both offerings like someone at a more advanced level. He pitches with a bulldog mentality, but controls his effort down the mound and has shown that he maintains his composure in big moments. Concerns about some reliever risk have dissipated, which should only help the Long Beach State recruit's Draft stock.

Christian Brothers HS (Memphis, Tenn.) has sent 11 players to the Majors, most notably All-Star catcher Tim McCarver. The Purple Wave now have the best prep catching prospect in the 2026 Draft after Brick reclassified from the 2027 class. He made that decision in October after starring for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in Japan, batting .333 while providing quality defense behind the plate as the second-youngest player on the squad. Brick's best tool is his well-above-average arm strength, as he regularly records sub-1.9-second pop times and can throw out basestealers from his knees. Gatorade's Tennessee high school player of the year, he moves well behind the plate and shows the potential to become a plus receiver and blocker once he improves his one-knee technique. He didn't have any issues handling the premium stuff he saw with the U.S. 18-and-under team and scouts rave about his makeup. Brick's bat hasn't been as good as anticipated this spring. The Mississippi State recruit has a quick right-handed stroke but gets too passive at times and his long levers result in some in-zone swing-and-miss worries. He displays plus raw power in batting practice but focuses more on hitting line drives during game action.

Sandefer's college passport has been well-stamped in Florida. He began his post-prep career at Division II St. Leo before moving to Central Florida and pitching in a bit of a swing role as a sophomore. He hit the transfer portal again and headed to the University of Florida, presumably for the chance to start. A minor injury had him working out of the pen to start the year and he didn't look comfortable, though he got in a groove over a couple of mid-week starts to earn a spot in the weekend rotation. That's been an up-and-down experience, especially in SEC play, and he seemed to dodge a bullet when x-rays came back negative after a comebacker hit him on his pitching arm during the conference tournament. While not the biggest right-hander in the world at 6-foot-1, Sandefer's stuff could give him the chance to start. He's seen his fastball tick upwards a bit this year, now sitting over 93 mph and touching 98 mph, and he backs it up with an interesting array of secondary offerings. He can miss bats with his low-80s slider with high spin, a breaker that can be a super-wide sweeper with angle, though it's inconsistent at times. He sells his low-80s changeup well with his arm speed and it features good fade and depth. He mixes in a cutter at times as well. All of Sandefer's repertoire comes from a really whippy arm and a low slot, with movement to everything he throws, and he's generally around the plate. His inconsistencies in conference play might have halted his helium a bit, but a team taking him in the top several rounds could send him out as a starter with the option to shorten him up for a life in the bullpen if that role doesn't stick.

The best Kansas prep position prospect since Bubba Starling went fifth overall to the Royals in 2011, Peterson won the High School Home Run Derby during All-Star Week and performed well at most showcase events last summer. He entered 2026 as one of the top power hitters in the high school class and won Gatorade's Kansas high school player of the year award, but he didn't drive the ball with authority as much this spring. He would draw some interest as a pitching prospect if he didn't have so much offensive potential. Peterson is employing a selective approach, keeping his left-handed swing under control and utilizing the entire field. He still possesses plus raw power but is focusing on making line-drive contract. Once he learns to drive balls in the air more regularly, he could produce 20-25 homers per season. Peterson has slowed down as he has gotten stronger and is now a below-average runner. There are mixed opinions about his defense at third base, with some scouts believing he's fine there and others questioning his athleticism and envisioning him as more of a corner outfielder. His arm strength is beyond reproach because the Texas recruit has been clocked up to 94 mph on the mound, where he also has displayed an interesting low-80s slider.

Conover was Cowley County (Kan.) CC's top hitter as a freshman in 2024, slashing .378/.508/.684, but his tendency to chase pitches limited him to part-time play last spring after he transferred to Oklahoma State. He toned down his approach as a junior and boosted his OPS from .843 to 1.101. He doesn't have a standout tool but also lacks a glaring weakness, and scouts love his makeup. Conover has a quick left-handed stroke but is content to work the middle of the field and drives more balls to left field with authority than he does to his pull side. He cut his chase rate from 26 percent in 2025 to 19 percent this spring, which made a huge difference because he rarely swings and misses against strikes, especially versus fastballs. The next adjustment will be to curb his tendency to make ground-ball contact, which cuts into what should be at least average power. Enhancing average speed with good instincts on the bases, Conover will pick his spots to steal and take extra bags. Primarily a left fielder for the Cowboys, he's an average defender with arm strength to match. He caught in high school and during fall practice, and the idea of moving him behind the plate intrigues some clubs.

One of the biggest wild cards in the Draft, Jelkin got dismissed from Nebraska as a freshman in 2022 and teams are still wary of his makeup. He spent 2023 at South Mountain (Ariz.) CC before blowing out his elbow at Houston the following spring, requiring Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of last season at Kentucky. He turned down the Dodgers as a 14th-rounder in 2023 and the Mets as a ninth-rounder in '24. Though he'll be 23 years and seven months old on Draft Day, he also has top two rounds stuff and earned second-team All-Southeastern Conference honors as a redshirt senior. Jelkin operates with three solid pitches with high spin rates, the best of which is a low-80s curveball with quality depth. His fastball has sat at 93-96 mph and reached 98 with power sink this spring, and it touched 100 during fall practice. His upper-80s cutter features late break that keeps it off barrels. Jelkin also shows some aptitude for a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink. A lanky 6-foot-5, 195-pounder with room to add more strength, he slings his pitches from a low three-quarters slot that adds deception. While he provides consistent strikes, he does catch the heart of the plate too often and will need to upgrade his command.

One of the more athletic and projectable pitchers in the 2026 high school crop, Putnam got a late start on the diamond this spring because he had to finish the basketball season first. His fastball touched 97 mph in his second outing, and while his breaking ball and control have been inconsistent, his arm talent is undeniable. He could take off once he focuses on baseball full-time and gets pro instruction, and his upside could land him in the top three rounds. When he's on, Putnam can work at 94-96 mph with armside run on his fastball, which has ranged from 88-98 during his senior season. Gatorade's 2026 Missouri high school player of the year, he can flash some solid upper-70s sliders with quality depth, though his breaker lacks reliability and needs more power. His mid-80s changeup has nice fade and is a more dependable offering. Putnam has a quick arm and a 6-foot-5 frame with plenty of room to add strength, so his pitches should gain more velocity in the future. The Tennessee recruit moves down the mound very well, creating extension that allows his stuff to get on hitters quicker than they expect. He'll scatter his pitches at times but has the ingredients for at least average control as he gains more experience.

After needing Tommy John surgery in high school that wiped out his senior year in Reno, Nev., Scolari also missed his true freshman year at San Diego in 2024 as he rehabbed. He returned as a Draft-eligible redshirt freshman in 2025, serving as the Toreros' Friday night starter and winning West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year honors. But he went undrafted and transferred to Oregon for 2026, where his improved stuff out of the gate had scouts bullish about him being a college performer who could go in the top few rounds. Missed time with arm issues made teams pause, but he did return and had a dominant five-inning, 10-strikeout shutout performance against Washington in Big 10 Conference Tournament play. Scolari is a big, strong right-hander standing at 6-foot-4 and 220 pounds, and when he's been healthy this year, his stuff has taken a big step forward from his year at San Diego. After sitting in the low-90s in 2025, he's averaged a touch over 94 mph this year, topping out at 98. His mid-80s slider is still his best secondary offering, missing bats at a 42-percent rate heading into Regional play thanks to good depth and tilt. He now also has a slower 80-mph curve that can elicit some swing-and-miss, and there's some feel for a firm changeup, but he doesn't throw it much. All of that, along with an overall solid delivery, gives Scolari a chance to start. His command is tracking in the right direction, with some thinking he'll be an average strike-thrower in time, but his lack of track record in consistently finding the zone along with the injury history does add some reliever risk to his profile.

Cuvet started establishing his power hitting bona fides during his high school days at ESB Academy south of Fort Lauderdale in Florida, even enticing the Pirates to take a flier on him in the 17th round of the 2023 Draft. He headed a little further south to Miami and immediately showed the pop would play in college, setting a Hurricanes freshman record with 24 home runs. He followed that up with 18 more in 2025, putting him in a tie for seventh all-time at the school heading into his junior year. Cuvet has established himself as a feared member of Miami's lineup, with perhaps as much raw power as anyone in the class. He can hit the ball out to all fields and even mis-hits balls over the fence. There are some holes in his swing, leading to some strikeout concerns, but he tends to cover the plate and has proven to be a decent two-strike hitter. If he can cut down the chase a bit, some feel he could approach being an average hitter, which means he might get to 70 in-game power. While he's not a bad athlete, especially for his size  he's close to an average runner underway  he has a bit of a slow motor at third base. So despite having an easily plus arm that fits at the hot corner, he's likely destined to move to the other infield corner, though a team could see if he could handle an outfield corner in a Nick Castellanos kind of way. Wherever he lands defensively, it's the power potential that will have teams calling in the top few rounds.

Murdock headed from the Utah high school ranks to UC San Diego, redshirting his freshman year and then spending his first real season on the mound in 2025 making eight Sunday starts and seven other relief outings, with mixed results. He was a Cape Cod League All-Star last summer, racking up eight saves as a closer for Orelans. He returned to the Tritons' rotation as a redshirt sophomore this spring and has shown glimpses of dominance, creating a buzz by outpitching Santa Barbara's Jackson Flora with an eight-inning, 17-strikeout masterpiece in early April, but then failed to build on that momentum in his next couple of outings. At his best, Murdock is a strong power pitcher who can maintain his stuff deep into starts, one who could pitch with two plus pitches at the next level. In that start against UCSB, he sat 95 mph and missed bats with the pitch, but while he's touched as high as 99 mph, he typically sits around 92-94 and it gets squared up. The slider is typically a legit out pitch, an 84-85 mph breaker that gets a ton of swings-and-misses along with chases. There's a mid-80s changeup in there, but he rarely goes to it, throwing his fastball-breaker almost all of the time. More often than not, Murdock's lack of command (well over five walks per nine in his college career), not to mention relatively low extension and effort in his delivery, leads to thoughts of reliever risk. A team interested in making him just the second Tritons pitcher to go in the top five rounds in over 50 years, joining Astros prospect Ryan Forcucci, could send him out as a starter while remembering just how good he looked coming out of the pen on the Cape.

A 20th-round pick out of a Virginia high school by the Guardians in 2023, Marohn pitched for the U.S. collegiate national team last summer and allowed just two earned runs in his first four starts this spring. He was building momentum toward the second round, but he missed his first start in March with biceps soreness and then went down in mid-April with a forearm strain. He didn't dominate as much in Atlantic Coast Conference action in between, further clouding his status. Marohn's fastball operates at 90-93 mph and peaks at 95, playing better than its velocity thanks to carry, command and deception. It works well with his best offering, a mid-80s changeup that induces a lot of chases with its tumble. His mid-70s curveball and low-80s slider flashed as solid pitches in 2025 but haven't been nearly as effective this year. Marohn's control has regressed as well, though he has continued to thrive while missing more bats than ever. He throws off hitters' timing with some crossfire in his delivery, funk in his arm action and wide angle. While his floor is more impressive than his ceiling, he could be a useful southpaw starter.

The son of former big league outfielder and current Oklahoma associate head coach Reggie Willits and the older brother of 2025 No. 1 overall pick Eli Willits, Jaxon could give his family a third potential big leaguer. He doesn't have a true standout tool but his high baseball IQ allows him to get the most out of his physical ability. Hitting .318 with more walks than strikeouts during two seasons in the wood-bat Cape Cod League helps bolster his case for going in the first three rounds, as did winning Most Outstanding Player honors while leading the Sooners to the 2026 College World Series championship. A switch-hitter, Willits makes more contact and hits the ball with more authority from the left side of the plate. He recognizes pitches well, doesn't chase and makes regular contact to all fields. He has average raw power and doesn't lift balls consistently, so he won't hit more than 12-15 homers per season. Willits is an opportunistic baserunner with average speed and quickness. He's more of a dependable than especially rangy shortstop, which along with his average arm strength makes him better equipped for second base. He's a high-floor utility type who draws universal praise for his intelligence and work ethic.

Sam Antonacci got his college start at Heartland (Ill.) CC before becoming a rookie sensation with the White Sox, and the Hawks have another middle-infield prospect. Anderson slashed .465/.544/1.030, leading Division II junior colleges in slugging and ranking fourth in homers (26 in 59 games). Headed to Kentucky if he doesn't turn pro, he has decent pop, solid speed and a future as a second baseman.

Hernandez registered on scouting radars as a Georgia prepster in 2024, but not enough for clubs to consider buying him away from Georgia Tech. He earned Atlantic Coast Conference freshman of the year accolades in 2025, starting games at six different spots (including one as a pitcher) and breaking Matt Wieters' freshman school record with 69 RBIs. Draft-eligible as a sophomore, he could factor in the top three rounds but also has struggled in ACC play and hasn't shown as much power this spring. Hernandez combines strength with good swing decisions to produce impressive exit velocities. But he also comes with some concerns at the plate, most notably his struggles to make contact against breaking balls. There's some arm bar in his right-handed stroke, which can get long and uphill, and he makes too much ground-ball contact while rarely pulling the ball. Though Hernandez has played a variety of positions, he's a below-average runner who's overmatched at second or third base. He's a fringy defender on the outfield corners and average at first. He does possess the arm strength for right field and pushed his fastball to 93 mph last year before concentrating on hitting as a sophomore.

Libbert appeared headed for the top three rounds as a Missouri high schooler in 2023 until he injured his elbow after slipping on artificial turf while making a throw and required Tommy John surgery. He redshirted at Missouri in 2024 and has produced more impressive stuff than results with the Tigers last year and with Mississippi this spring. He pitched his way out of the Rebels' Southeastern Conference rotation after just two starts but can look like a second-round talent with four viable offerings at his best. Libbert has raised his arm slot to improve the carry on his fastball, which averages 95 mph and reaches 98 but gets hammered when he doesn't locate it well. His mid-80s cutter has been his best pitch this year, showing more consistency than his low-80s slider with horizontal and vertical action. His mid-80s changeup tumbles when it's working but has regressed. Working from a higher slot has cost Libbert life on his fastball and Mississippi has called for his secondary pitches more than his heater. His proponents think lowering his arm angle, restoring the previous tempo in his delivery and re-establishing his fastball could lead to success as a starter, while other evaluators project him as more of a multi-inning lefty reliever. He still works with some effort and will need to improve his control and command.

A Tucson native who attended Suaharita HS south of the Arizona city, Kramkowski stayed put to play for the University of Arizona in college. He pitched sparingly as a freshman in 2024, then spent his sophomore year in the Wildcats' weekend rotation. There was some buzz this fall as his velocity ticked upward, but he hasn't maintained the better stuff as Arizona's Friday starter during his junior year this spring. With his tall, thin frame and glimpses of an easy fastball, Kramkowski has drawn some comps to T.J. Nichols, a former Arizona hurler and current Rays prospect. The 6-foot-3 right-hander relies mostly on his sinking fastball-slider combination. It's a bowling ball heater that was up to 98 mph this fall, but was back around the 92-93 range he threw it in as a starter in 2025, and it does elicit very high ground-ball rates. He backs it up with an upper-70s slider that has decent three-quarter traditional tilt to it. He started going to his average mid-80s cutter more frequently this spring. Kramkowski threw a ton of strikes last year, walking only 1.8 per nine. He repeated that in 2026, but it's control over command, and at times, he can get too much of the plate and get hit. Teams might pick apart his lack of a put-away heater or his lack of secondary pitch metrics, but he has been posting every week and the sinker-slider combination gives him some building blocks to work with on the pro side.

Randall was a standout at Northern California high school power De La Salle (a program known for producing lefty Kyle Harrison), but he pulled his name out of the 2023 Draft because he was intent on attending UCLA. After pitching infrequently as a freshman, Randall has been a mainstay in the Bruins' bullpen. Though he's never closed, he's shown his power stuff can dominate top college hitters, leading him to an eye-popping 16.5 K/9 rate and .142 batting average against in his junior year. A 6-foot-4 right-hander, Randall is all about his fastball. To say he's heater-heavy would be a huge understatement as he threw the pitch -- averaging close to 97 mph and touching triple digits -- 89 percent of the time this spring. It is an extremely effective pitch, but not just because of the velocity. It elicited a 36 percent miss rate this season thanks to a combination of low release and extension to create upshoot arm side life. He basically throws one secondary pitch, an 89-92 mph slider-cutter hybrid that can be effective because it's hard, but it's also short and some think he'll need to come up with something that features more depth at the next level. The other challenge Randall faces is his ability to throw strikes, as he walked 5.4 per nine over his college career at UCLA. He won't need pinpoint command to be a big league reliever, but a team taking him will hope he can find a little better feel for the zone and add shape to his secondary offering in order to grow into a high-leverage role.

A solid high school prospect from Dunedin, Florida, Beard began his college career in state at Florida Atlantic University, stepping right into the Owls rotation as a freshman. He took a big step forward as their sophomore ace in 2025, earning All American Athletic Conference First Team honors in the process before making a couple of Cape Cod League appearances and participating in USA Baseball's Collegiate National Training Camp over the summer. A transfer to Florida State and the ACC could help his profile. Tall and lean, Beard is the quintessential pitchability college lefty with a strong feel for his craft and an unusual delivery to help it all play up. Everything comes from a very high slot that creates extension and deception. Velocity-wise, his fastball is fringy, sitting around 90-91 mph and topping out at 94, but he does a nice job of elevating it up and hitters chasing it out of the zone. His best pitch is his 75-77 mph changeup that gets Bugs Bunny comments from scouts, sold with outstanding arm speed. He has feel for spinning his breaking stuff with some depth, both a newer low-80s slider and a softer curve he's had since his prep days, though they trail the cambio so he uses them a bit more strategically. Beard has made excellent strides with his ability to fill up the zone and limit walks. His ceiling might be a bit limited, but he's reminded some of Guardians lefty Logan Allen, a second rounder out of Florida International in 2020, in terms of the path he could potentially follow.

Nevada's best prep pitching prospect in 2023, Mercurius spent his first two college seasons at Nevada-Las Vegas before transferring to Oklahoma to reunite with his brother Xander, the Silver State's top high school arm in 2025. L.J. can look like a second-round talent at his best and opened this spring by allowing one earned run in four non-conference starts before pitching his way out of the rotation by mid-May. He played a key bullpen role for the Sooners and won the clinching game at the College World Series. Mercurius operates with a 92-94 mph fastball that peaks at 97 with improved carry but not much running action, so it gets in trouble when he doesn't locate it well. The same is true with his mid-80s changeup, a plus offering with fade and sink that was victimized for five homers in his first seven SEC starts. He relies primarily on those two pitches while mixing in some tight low-80s sliders. The Sooners have raised Mercurius' arm slot to get more backspin on his fastball, similar to what they did with first-rounder Kyson Witherspoon in 2025. He's throwing more strikes as a junior than he did last year but his ability to improve his command will determine his future success. If he can't, he'll be more middle reliever than No. 4 starter.

Anderson is actually a two-way player, but he tore his UCL and only hit this year as a senior at Penn State. After two years at Rhode Island and one at Arkansas, he slashed .358/.470/.742 with 20 homers for the Nittany Lions this year. A team could take him and let him, hit, knowing that he was up to 99 mph with his fastball in the fall before the elbow injury.

The son of 1994 seventh overall pick Trot Nixon, who played 12 seasons in the big leagues, Luke is an undersized, scrappy second baseman who can handle the bat and has a high baseball IQ. He batted .367/.452/.595 with nine homers and 11 steals and could have a future as a utilityman.

Tennessee's top prep prospect in 2023, McElvain went undrafted because he was intent on following in the footsteps of his older brother Chris (now in the Blue Jays system) and attending Vanderbilt. He compiled a 5.33 ERA in two years with the Commodores before transferring to Arkansas and enjoying much more success. He logged a 1.88 ERA and 34 percent strikeout rate while establishing himself as one of the top lefty relievers in the Draft. McElvain is throwing a tick harder this season, working with a 94-96 mph fastball that peaks at 98 and is most effective when he locates it with carry up in the zone. The Razorbacks have had him employ his heater more than ever and mostly shelve the slider and curveball he used at Vanderbilt. He mainly complements his fastball with a cutter that averages 89 mph and touches 92, tying up both lefties and righties. Arkansas has streamlined McElvain's delivery, helping him repeat it more easily while still preserving much of its funk. He has cut his 17 percent walk rate at Vandy in half this spring, though his command still wavers at times. He's purely a reliever but has the stuff and mentality to handle a late-inning role.

McNeillie was the top high school pitcher in Georgia in 2023, but went undrafted because he was intent on fulfilling his commitment to the University of Florida. He was an intriguing combination of projection and polish when he got to campus and three years later, scouts are still trying to figure out who he is as a pitcher. He's thrown almost entirely as a reliever, showing off premium stuff at times but not with results that have always matched it. There was hope the 6-foot-3 McNeillie would take to a starting role at some point with the Gators, but while that hasn't come to pass, some feel he should be given a chance to do so as a pro. His stuff is louder in shorter stints out of the bullpen, starting with a fastball that's been 96-99 mph this year as a reliever. It can have some carry when it's at the top of the zone, and there's some occasional, perhaps unintentional, two-seam action because his delivery pulls him open and he drops his slot, but it's often too straight and gets hit more than it should. His best and most-frequently thrown pitch is his 86-88 mph slider and it flashes plus, with good downer action to it when it's on. There is a changeup in there, but he doesn't use it often. McNeillie's command in and out of the zone has been spotty at Florida and that, along with a lack of extension or deception, makes it tougher to project what he might be at the next level. He can get caught between trying to be a complete pitcher and attacking with his power stuff. There will be teams interested in his arm strength, with one good at pitching development perhaps working with him on starting long-term.

Because he's one of the older legitimate prospects in the 2026 high school class -- 19 years and five months old on Draft Day -- Bowen creates some mixed opinions among evaluators. Some believe his mix of tools and potential to stay at shortstop could merit a third-round pick if he's signable. In large part because of his age, others would rather see him prove himself for two years at Oklahoma State before making a significant investment. Bowen has a simple right-handed stroke that he repeats well while focusing on producing line drives from gap to gap. He has the bat speed to catch up to quality velocity and makes consistent contact. He doesn't show much present raw power and generates a lot of grounders, so he may top out at 12-15 homers per season. Bowen has plus speed that translates into base-stealing ability and range at shortstop. He has solid arm strength and should be able to remain at short. His athleticism and arm give him the versatility to play almost anywhere on the diamond.

Moore wasn't a blue-chip recruit as an Ohio high schooler but has blossomed into one of the most dangerous basestealers in college baseball. A part-time player as a freshman in 2024, he led NCAA Division I with 53 steals in 54 attempts as a sophomore and topped the Atlantic Coast Conference with 37 in 44 tries this spring. His favorite player is Orioles 2023 first-rounder Enrique Bradfield and their games are similar. Moore doesn't quite have Bradfield's top-of-the-scale speed but he's a plus-plus runner who uses his speed to get on base and create havoc. He doesn't rely purely on his quickness, studying pitchers and getting good jumps as a basestealer and showing good reads and routes while playing a quality center field. His arm is merely fringy but more than enough for his position. A left-handed hitter with little power, Moore understands his limitations and leans into his strengths. He controls the strike zone and makes consistent contact, though his strikeout rate rose from 11 percent in 2025 to 16 percent this year. He doesn't try to hit the ball in air, concentrating on line drives and grounders he can beat out with his speed, and he draws his share of walks.

Guyette attended training camp with the U.S. collegiate national team last summer and scouts like the east-west contrast of his heavy 92-94 mph sinker that peaks at 97 and his low-80s slider. He can evade barrels with his fading low-80s changeup as well. He fashioned a 5.56 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 79 1/3 innings as a junior.

After compiling a 3.36 ERA in two seasons as a starter at Seminole State (Okla.) JC, Dahl transferred to Louisiana Tech. Conference USA's 2026 newcomer of the year, he posted the best ERA (2.11) and strikeout total (73) in C-USA play this spring. His polish and metrics stand out more than stuff, and he intrigues clubs confident in their ability to help pitchers add power. Dahl did pick up 2 mph on his fastball this spring, working at 91-93 mph, topping out at 95 and succeeding with fringy velocity thanks to an unusually low release height and flat approach angle. His low-80s changeup sinks under barrels, though he can struggle to land it for strikes. His tight low-80s slider is less effective and gets drilled when he leaves it over the plate. Dahl's low arm slot creates plenty of deception that leads hitters to chase all of his pitches off the plate. He doesn't land any of his offerings in the zone on a regular basis, yet they all generate plenty of strikes. He'll be a fun development project for whichever team drafts him.

The younger brother of Brewers left-hander Kyle Harrison, Bear is an offensive-minded catcher who offers on-base skills (41 walks, 22 hit by pitches in 52 games) and right-handed pop. He batted .294/.493/.608 with 11 homers and is still a work in progress behind the plate.

Gasparino was one of a handful of the top 100 on MLB Pipeline's Draft Top 250 Prospects list in 2023 to go undrafted and head to college. The son of Dodgers long-time scouting executive Billy Gasparino, Will spent his first two years struggling at the University of Texas. A transfer to UCLA and a subsequent change to his setup at the plate unlocked a lot of offensive potential and helped vault him into early-round conversations. Even back in his high school years, Gasparino was a huge tower of raw tools. The 6-foot-6 right-handed hitter is capable of hitting the ball as hard and as far as just about anyone in the class. At Texas, he was more spread out in the box, and he never got comfortable. At UCLA, he's gone back to something closer to what he did in high school, a bit more upright where he feels he can be more athletic. It's provided more consistent results, though there will always be swing-and-miss in his game, with skeptics fearing his tendency to chase will keep him from producing and tapping into his double plus raw power at the next level. While Gasparino is an above-average runner, he hasn't used that speed to steal bases in college. It does help him play an above-average center field, where his strong arm is also an asset. The team that takes him in the top few rounds will be the one who thinks he can refine his approach just enough to reach his ceiling as a hitter.

As a Florida high school right-hander with pitchability and a quality changeup, Knaak could have gone in the top five rounds of the 2023 Draft, but he didn't command a high enough bonus to give up on attending Clemson. He became the first pitcher in Tigers history to earn all-Atlantic Coast Conference first-team recognition in each of his first two seasons, as well as the first to reach 100 strikeouts in each of his first two years. But his stuff and strike-throwing regressed this spring, when he got pounded for a 5.81 ERA. Knaak has advanced feel for his changeup, varying the velocity from the low 70s to the mid 80s while imparting plenty of fade and tumble, though it wasn't quite as dominant in 2026 as it had been in the past. His cambio helps him compensate for the lack of velocity and life on a 91-93 mph fastball that tops out at 96, and his heater plays up a bit because he commands it well. He doesn't show much aptitude for spin, however, and opponents raked at a .476/.500/.714 clip against his tight mid-80s slider and low-80s curveball this spring. Knaak does a good job of working around the edges of the strike zone with his fastball while setting hitters up for his changeup, but his lack of a breaking ball caught up to him as a junior. His delivery and control weren't as smooth as usual, which compounded his problems. While he lacks size and projection, he's strong and competitive and could become a back-of-the-rotation starter if he can regain his previous form.

A legitimate two-way player from the New Jersey high school ranks, Weingartner didn't register all that much on the summer showcase circuit, playing sparingly at the East Coast Pro Showcase and both pitching and hitting some at the Area Code Games. He started generating some buzz this winter when he broke the record with a 6.24-second 60-yard dash at the Prep Baseball Report Super 60 and continued to build a case for himself, more as a position player than a pitcher, as the top prep player in the Garden State this spring. While he can crank his fastball up to 94-96 mph on the mound at times, it's Weingartner's athleticism and tools as a position player that was garnering more attention this spring. He can put on a show in batting practice, with clear raw power from the right side of the plate. He's shown some feel in games, but there is some length to what looks like a bit of a manufactured swing that some evaluators think might struggle with premium velocity from professional pitching. It's obvious that Weingartner has plus speed, and the arm that can touch mid-90s as a pitcher works from shortstop. He could be the type of high school athlete who might need a couple of summers in a complex league, and it remains to be seen if a team will be willing to spend to keep him from honoring his commitment to Penn State.

Fay gradually has improved throughout his four years at Alabama, which began with redshirting as a walk-on in 2023 and taking his lumps as a reliever the following spring. He worked his way into the Crimson Tide's weekend rotation midway through last year, when he could have gotten drafted in the 7th-10th round if he had been signable there. After going unselected, he became the No. 1 starter on a College World Series team in 2026 and threw a 13-strikeout no-hitter against Florida in March. Fay doesn't light up radar guns, but he pounds the strike zone with a fastball that sits at 91-93 mph and reaches 97 wit h run, sink and deception. He uses his heater to set up his best pitch, a sweeping slider that parks around 80 mph and works against both left-handers and right-handers. He'll need a better third offering at the next level because neither his low-80s changeup nor his mid-80s cutter fools enough hitters. The 6-foot-5 Fay uses his lanky frame and low arm slot to create a flat approach angle and wide release that are especially tough on righties. His lack of velocity leaves him more vulnerable to lefties, against whom he must command his arsenal well to succeed. He has no difficulty providing strikes but sometimes catches too much of the plate.

A redshirt junior who spent his first two college seasons at South Carolina-Aiken, Byrd starred in the postseason as Georgia finished third at the College World Series. His 93-95 mph fastball peaks at 97 and is difficult to hit at the top of strike zone, while his low-80s slider has plenty of sweep. He has some aptitude for throwing a mid-80s changeup as well, so a pro team may try to start him after he logged a 3.73 ERA with eight saves, a .194 opponent average and 77/14 K/BB ratio in 62 2/3 innings.

Adams looked like a potential 2025 first-rounder based on how he pitched during the fall leading into that season, but struggled as a sophomore and went undrafted. He bounced back as the Saturday starter on Alabama's College World Series team this year, compiling a 4.58 ERA with 100 strikeouts in 90 1/3 innings. He operates with a 91-94 mph fastball that touches 96, has flashed a plus upper-70s curveball and shows good feel for a 77-81 mph changeup that dies at the plate.

Sosa was a solid high school prospect on the east coast of Florida who was in the top 125 of MLB Pipeline's Draft Top 250 back in 2023. He went undrafted and headed to North Carolina State to begin his college career, spending two years with the Wolfpack before being considered one of the best players, especially behind the plate, in the transfer portal. He came back home, fulfilling a dream to play for Miami for his junior season, putting up excellent numbers for the Hurricanes. There were two big questions surrounding Sosa when he got to Miami: Can he hit for average and can he catch? He's improved on both fronts this spring to improve his Draft stock. Scouts have some conviction his left-handed swing will play at the next level, with what is now a solid gap-to-gap approach. He has very good raw power to his pull side that he's been getting to in games, while also showing this season that he can handle left-handed pitching, cutting down his strikeout rate and drawing more walks. Sosa still has work to do in his overall defense behind the dish, but he has made strides in his blocking and does a good job of framing and stealing strikes. He has fringy arm strength which can play up as average at times because of his quick release. He has the floor of being a solid backup or platoon type, with the ceiling of being an every day, bat-first catcher.

When Chris Pollard left Duke to take over as the head coach at the University of Virginia in the summer of 2025, seven players followed him via the transfer portal. The marquee name was first-round candidate AJ Gracia, but it also included Johnson, a two-way player with more upside on the mound. A strong fall had scouts in the area excited about what he might be able to do as a pitcher for the Cavaliers, but he was slowed out of the gate by what was termed a kinetic chain issue, and he didn't make his first appearance until March 20. As he has throughout his college career, he put up inconsistent numbers on the bump. Despite a less-than-pretty statline, scouts are still bullish on Johnson as an athletic left-hander who has yet to focus on pitching full-time. He has as many as five pitches to work with, starting with a fastball that averaged a touch over 93 mph but topped out at 97-98 mph this spring, and it some ride to it when he's at the top of the zone. His slider, thrown up to 83-84 mph, can be a 1-to-7, hammer-like breaker with a ton of swing and miss. He has a distinct upper-70s curve and can also throw a harder, 86-88 mph cutter. He used his low-80s changeup more than any other secondary pitch, throwing it downhill with armside sink and run, a cambio he'll throw to hitters on both sides of the plate. Johnson has never been a consistent strike-thrower, carrying a career 4.6 BB/9 (5.1 per nine in 2026) rate into NCAA Regional play this year. But there are some raw ingredients to work with, and there were teams who felt he was worthy of top five round consideration, with perhaps another gear to reach when he puts the bat down for good.

People who say the path to professional baseball can be long and winding might have had Worley in mind. The St. Louis area native originally committed to Missouri for college ball, but switched gears and went the junior college route, heading to Amarillo College in Texas. From there, he headed west and threw well at Modesto Junior College, which helped him land a spot at Stony Brook University. After struggling with strikes and not getting a lot of mound time as a junior, the left-hander took a big step forward as the Seawolves' Friday night starter in 2026, making him a potentially intriguing senior sign option. Worley's combination of size (6-foot-5), arm strength and left-handedness is sure to intrigue teams on Day 2. He'll throw his fastball anywhere in the 92-99 mph range with good shapes. That plus heater was on display at the MLB Draft Combine in June, where he was up to 98 mph with nearly 20 inches of vertical break. He backs up that fastball with a hard low-80s slider that flashes plus and missed a ton of bats in 2026 -- 46 percent according to Synergy -- and he can also fold in an occasional upper-70s curve. He rarely threw his low-80s changeup, but he wants to make it a regular part of his arsenal as a pro. Adding that offspeed pitch and continuing to refine his command will be the keys for him to have a chance to keep starting at the next level. His improved strike-throwing was encouraging and a team could certainly give him the chance to stick in a rotation, knowing the fastball-slider combination from the left side could be dominant in shorter relief stints.

After going undrafted as a Nevada high schooler and then in two seasons at Mesa (Ariz.) CC and his first at McNeese State, Nachtsheim has emerged as one of the best college senior prospects in 2026. Though the Cowboys bounced him between closing and starting depending on team need this spring, he set a school record with 129 strikeouts in 93 innings and led NCAA Division I with 98 K's via the heater. McNeese State's best pitching prospect since 2005 first-rounder Jacob Marceaux, Nachtsheim finished the season by allowing just eight runs in five starts. Nachtsheim's fastball parks at 92-94 mph and peaks at 97 while featuring some of the best carry in the Draft, as well as some natural cutting action. He throws his heater three-quarters of the time, utilizing a lackluster low-80s slider as his main secondary option. His fading low-80s changeup works as a chase pitch, but he has trouble landing it in the zone and it often gets hammered when he does. Scouts don't love Nachtsheim's less-than-smooth delivery and arm action, though they don't prevent him from filling the strike zone. He does create quality extension that adds to the deception with his fastball. While he'll likely get the chance to show what he can do as a starter in pro ball, his long-term future almost certainly is as a reliever.

Part of a deeper than usual New York prep pitching crop in 2023 that also included Brewers supplemental first-rounder Josh Knoth and future North Carolina ace Jason DeCaro, LeGuernic deflected interest from pro clubs to attend Clemson. He logged an 8.62 ERA in his first two years with the Tigers before cutting that mark to 4.69 as a full-time reliever as a junior. Scouts believe he has a lot of untapped potential, so he could go a few rounds earlier than his performance might indicate. LeGuernic owns one of the more unhittable sliders in the college class, a mid-80s breaker with high spin rates and huge sweeping action. His fastball operates in the mid 90s and touches 98 mph with carry and armside run, though right-handers crush it more than they should. Both pitches added 3-4 mph this spring. He doesn't have much faith in an upper-80s changeup with mild fade that he can't land in the zone often enough to tempt hitters. Working from an extremely low arm slot gives LeGuernic deception as well as sweep on his slider, though it also hampers his control and command. His quick arm and 6-foot-4 frame have some scouts wondering if he could succeed as a starter in pro ball, though he'd need to do a better job of locating his pitches and refine his changeup. It's more realistic to project him as a slider-happy reliever who can carve up left-handers.

Elbow issues that included a stress fracture that required surgery limited Petrovic to 29 2/3 innings in his first two seasons with the Tigers before he stayed healthy and became one of the top Sunday starters in college baseball as a redshirt sophomore. He went 10-2 with a 3.21 ERA, .207 opponent average and 92 strikeouts in 92 2/3 innings. He's a finesse righty with a low-90s fastball that reaches 96 mph and a quality low-80s changeup with fade and sink.

Addari redshirted at Michigan State in 2024 and worked just 17 2/3 innings at Illinois State last spring before breaking out and leading the Missouri Valley Conference with a 2.41 ERA this year. He posted a 73/22 K/BB ratio in 67 1/3 innings while displaying a 92-95 mph fastball that touched 98 with heavy sink and a low-80s slider. His low release height and the extension in his delivery are two more points in his favor, and he also stood out in athletic testing at the MLB Draft Combine.

Marsten overcame Tommy John surgery as a high school sophomore to reach 99 mph and generate top-three-rounds buzz at baseball power Harvard-Westlake (Studio City, Calif.) in 2024, though he went undrafted because of his commitment to Wake Forest. His career with the Demon Deacons hasn't played out as hoped, as he got hammered as a little-used reliever as a freshman and pitched his way out of the Atlantic Coast Conference rotation after just two starts this spring. He performed much better as a midweek starter but has the stuff to be much more than that. Marsten can miss bats with all four of his pitches, beginning with a 94-96 mph fastball that tops out at 99 with carry and armside run. He uses a tight mid-80s slider as his primary secondary pitch against right-handers and switches to a slightly harder cutter versus left-handers, with both grading as solid offerings. His fading changeup is tough to barrel but he shows little feel for locating it. This season, Marsten has dominated righties but gotten crushed by lefties, who tee off on his fastball because he can't land his cutter and changeup for strikes on a regular basis. He has a strong 6-foot-3, 220-pound build and offers the potential of a mid-rotation starter with three plus pitches but also little track record to suggest he can get there. It's unclear whether he'd be better off getting his pro career started now or returning to college and trying to rebuild his stock as a junior.

A native of Quebec, Lachance slammed 31 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC before transferring to Oklahoma. He didn't go deep in his first 31 games for the Sooners this spring before doing so 18 times in his final 33 contests. Oklahoma rallied from an 11th-place finish in the Southeastern Conference to win its third national title, with Lachance homering six times and driving in 18 runs in 13 NCAA tournament games. Lachance creates well-above-average raw power that plays to all fields with a combination of bat speed, strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-5, 231-pound frame. He has a sound right-handed swing but his 36 percent chase rate ranked among the highest in NCAA Division I and is a cause for concern. He's extremely vulnerable against breaking balls out of the zone but hammers curveballs and sliders that venture over the plate. Lachance possesses little speed and is a station-to-station runner on the bases. He opened this season playing more first base before taking over at catcher for the Sooners in the second half. Despite his size and lack of quickness, he moves decently behind the plate and gets the job done as a catcher, though he can be overly aggressive trying to frame pitches. He has solid-to-plus arm strength but could improve his transfer and throwing accuracy.

A high school teammate in Hawaii of current Marlins prospect Aiva Arquette, Contrades earned state Gatorade Player of the Year honors before heading to Arizona State. After a solid freshman year that saw him earn an all-conference honorable mention nod, he missed nearly all of the 2024 season with a back injury. Contrades hit well, albeit without a ton of impact, upon his return in 2025, a season cut a month short because of a broken hand. While a hamstring injury slowed him in 2026, Contrades led all Division I second basemen with 21 homers, earning second-team All-American status from both Baseball America and the ABCA. An undersized infielder who hits right-handed, Contrades has shown off impressive bat-to-ball skills when he's been on the field since his freshman year. He struck out just 13 percent of the time in 2025 and 2026 combined while walking 10.8 percent of the time. He's always been happy to send hard line drives to all fields, but this year he started getting to his power, finding the seats in all directions, but particularly to his pull side. In the past, Contrades has shown plus run times, though the hamstring issue slowed him down a bit this spring, and he should settle in as an above-average runner. He's played third for the Sun Devils in the past but has settled in as a second baseman, probably his best spot should he develop into a regular at one position, with an average glove and arm. His positional limitation and the fact he's a 22-year-old redshirt junior are the two things that limit his helium.

A product of the Oregon high school ranks, Molony stayed in state for college ball. He made an immediate impact at University of Oregon, earning freshman All-American and first-team all-Pac 12 honors after finishing with a .969 OPS. He duplicated that OPS effort as a sophomore, finishing with 15 homers and 10 steals. A rough stint in the Cape Cod League didn't help his overall profile, but he's still the best prospect in the Pacific Northwest. While he's not in the same category as Aiva Arquette, the Oregon State shortstop who was the No. 7 overall pick in the 2025 Draft, Molony has plenty of attributes to like. The right-handed hitter produces plenty of bat speed coming from a strong and athletic 6-foot-2 frame. The power continues to come, especially to his pull side, though his inability to get to it with a wood bat on the Cape concerns some scouts. He rarely swings and misses at in-zone offerings, but not everyone is sold on his pure hit tool to get to that power. Most evaluators give Molony the chance to stick at shortstop. He's average, maybe a tick above, as a runner, but he has solid range, good hands and more than enough arm for the premium position. He's unlikely to reach Arquette levels come Draft time, but a strong junior season with the Ducks could vault him into first-round conversations.

Morton damaged tendons in his throwing wrist while hitting fungoes as a Minnesota high school senior in 2023, so he made just two starts at the beginning of that season -- and reached 97 mph with his fastball and 91 with his cutter. He turned down a lucrative offer from the Brewers in the 19th around to attend Texas A&M, where he worked just 19 1/3 innings in two years while battling the strike zone and an oblique injury. After transferring back home, he became Minnesota's best pitching prospect since 2020 No. 3 overall pick Max Meyer before blowing out his elbow in his final regular-season start and requiring Tommy John surgery. Morton generates premium stuff from a sidearm slot and low release height, creating plenty of run and sink on a fastball that operates at 93-95 mph and touches 97. He produces premium spin rates on a mid-80s slider with excessive sweep and a cutter that parks in the low 90s. His firm upper-80s changeup features some fade but doesn't fool hitters. While Morton displayed much better control than he did with the Aggies, he caught the heart of the plate too often. None of his offerings elicit many chases because he throws so many strikes, and only his slider qualifies as a swing-and-miss pitch (while his sinker is valuable because it generates so much groundball contact). He doesn't have a weapon to get lefties out, though better command could help.

Winslow played two years at Duke before joining North Carolina and slashing .282/.417/.466 with 10 homers in 68 games for the College World Series runners-up. He has solid to plus bat speed and raw power to go with a strong arm, though his receiving skills needs improvement.

After breaking Mark Reynolds' Virginia freshman home run record with 17, Ford ranked as one of the top sophomore-eligible prospects in the 2025 Draft. He slashed .362/.420/.575 with 11 homers last spring, but the dip in power left teams unwilling to meet his asking price, so he transferred to Tennessee after going unpicked. He could land in the top three or four rounds after trading some contact for pop this spring while moving to third base. Ford made more consistent contact as a sophomore but didn't hit balls as hard as he did as a freshman, and he has struck a better balance as a junior. He doesn't have the prettiest swing and is overly aggressive at the plate, yet he always produces. The strength and leverage in his right-handed stroke give him plus raw power, mostly to his pull side but occasionally to the opposite field, though he doesn't lift balls consistently and may top out at 20 homers per season. The 6-foot-5, 220-pound Ford is a below-average runner but a decent athlete for his size. Primarily a first baseman as a freshman, he played a credible right field with average arm strength as a sophomore and even manned center field in the Cape Cod League. He lacks the quickness for the hot corner, so his best-case scenario in pro ball is probably left field.

Burdette won the Ohio Division I championship at Moeller HS (Cincinnati) in 2023, when he ranked as the third-best prep shortstop in the state behind Colt Emerson and A.J. Ewing. He went to Ohio State but redshirted for a season before transferring to Xavier, where he totaled 30 homers and 23 steals in the last two seasons. With one of the best combinations of physicality (6-foot-2, 215 pounds) and athleticism in the college class, he could surpass 2017 eighth-rounder Rylan Bannon as the highest-drafted position player in Musketeers history. Burdette's strength and bat speed generate higher exit velocities than most players in NCAA Division I. He has well-above-average raw power and mainly drives balls from gap to gap, and he could tap into his pop even more if he turns on and launches more pitches. A right-handed hitter, he comes with questions about his hitting ability because he hasn't faced much quality pitching. His aggressive approach results in a lot of chases and strikeouts and very few walks. At least a plus runner, Burdette can use his quickness to beat out infield hits and steal bases. He also covers more ground than most right fielders and has the solid arm strength for the position. He has the speed to warrant a shot at center field at the next level.

Peterson pushed his fastball to 94 mph as a Tennessee high school senior in 2023 but was still raw on the mound, so he headed to Walters State (Tenn.) CC. He helped the Senators finish second at the 2025 Junior College World Series before transferring to Appalachian State, where he was named Sun Belt Conference Newcomer of the Year in '26. He notched 107 strikeouts (second-most in school history) in 85 innings and blanked Men's College World Series participant Troy for seven innings in May. Though Peterson still tops out at 94 mph and his heater sits at 91-92, it generates plenty of chases and empty swings because it comes out of a high arm slot with tough carry at times and steep downhill plane at others. None of his secondary pitches stand out, with his low-80s changeup with depth more effective than his breaking balls. His low-80s slider works better than his 75-78 mph curveball. Peterson's metrics pop more than his stuff, as he uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create an unusually high and wide release point, and also some natural extension. He lacks a smooth arm action and consistent timing in his delivery, so he'll battle the strike zone on occasion. If a pro team can help him increase his velocity and refine a complementary option, he'll have a plus fastball and a better chance to succeed as a starter.

A two-sport athlete who starred on the diamond and gridiron during his high school days in San Diego, Bayles headed north to Santa Clara to focus on pitching. He made an immediate impact as a reliever who collected five saves and was named to the West Coast Conference All-Freshman Team. He was an all-WCC Second Team honoree in 2025, spending most of the season in the rotation, then rose to first-team status this spring while serving as the Broncos' Friday night starter, leading all WCC starters in ERA (2.54) and batting average against. Bayles' best offering is by far his high-spin slider. The 6-foot-3 right-hander throws the low-80s breaker more than this fastball and it features power and depth, eliciting a 50 percent miss rate this season, according to Synergy. He tunnels it well with his fastball, making it even harder to pick up. His heater is much more pedestrian, a pitch that tops out at 94 mph and sits around 91, but he struggles to command it with an over-the-top delivery that leads to poor release traits. He has a changeup that has a chance to be a decent third pitch, but he rarely throws it. The combination of his delivery and spotty command and control -- he walked 4.6 per nine in his college career, a rate that rose to 5.6 as a junior -- not to mention the lack of confidence in a third pitch, point to a future as a reliever for Bayles. A team could send him out as a starter and see if he can iron out some of those flaws, knowing that plus slider could look very good coming out of a bullpen.

Piech missed his first season at Xavier following Tommy John surgery and bounced back from hip labrum surgery last fall to open 2026 with three strong road starts at East Carolina, Arkansas and Cal State Fullerton. Working with a 92-94 mph fastball that features good carry and an 82-85 mph slider, he led the Big East Conference in strikeout rate (11.6 per nine innings) and opponent average (.201).

More athletic than most catchers, Brenner can flash some plus run times and moves well behind the plate, where he displays solid arm strength. An Oklahoma recruit, he has a compact right-handed stroke and a line-drive approach.

Rice would be a lock to go in the top two or three rounds if not for his lack of physicality and his commitment to Auburn, but his combination of a deep arsenal and polish gives him plenty of believers among evaluators. He's built along the lines of Tim Hudson and his style is reminiscent of the four-time All-Star. He drove in both runs in the Georgia 3-A championship game to lead Pickens HS to its first-ever state title. Rice's best pitch is a tight mid-80s slider with high spin rates, but it's just one of four weapons at his disposal. His fastball sits in the low 90s, touches 95 and misses bats with its carry and armside run. His feel to spin extends to a low-80s curveball that he lands in the zone, and he also shows advanced aptitude for a fading mid-80s changeup. Rice has an up-tempo delivery but the athleticism to repeat it well and throw strikes with all four of his offerings. He generates his stuff with a quick arm and has a track record of performing against top competition. Though he's undersized at 5-foot-11, he has the potential to become a mid-rotation starter.

Born in Panama City, Guevara was Panama's top hitter at the 18-and-under World Cup in 2022 before his senior season at Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro). Knee injuries limited him in his first two seasons at Auburn, but he was one of the best all-around players in the Southeastern Conference this spring. He batted .322/.399/.533 with 13 homers and earned SEC all-defensive honors at third base for the second straight year. Though Guevara has been productive with metal bats and generates good exit velocities, there are some questions about how he'll perform at the next level with wood. The right-handed hitter almost never turns on pitches, produces little power against quality fastballs and makes inconsistent contact against breaking balls and changeups. He has an aggressive approach and mainly concentrates on drilling line drives from gap to gap. An average runner, Guevara plays quicker than that at the hot corner. He's an agile defender with solid to plus arm strength, and he got the job done when he opened this season at shortstop. He also has seen action at second base and left field during his college career.

After pitching sparingly as a freshman at Oklahoma in 2023, Turnquist transferred to Cal Poly but ended up redshirting in '24 following Tommy John surgery. He barely pitched in '25 but landed in the Mustangs’ rotation in '26, striking out 10.8 per nine, earning All-Big West Second Team honors and winning big games in the Big West Conference Tournament and NCAA Regional play. He’s a 6-foot-5 right-hander with a fastball he can run up to 98 mph, a low-80s slider that can miss bats and a mid-80s changeup, though command issues might point to a future in the bullpen.

Bryans makes it tough on left-handers with a very low arm slot and wide angle that produces fastballs that reach 98 mph and sliders that top out at 91. His sinking low-80s changeup keeps right-handers at bay. A two-way player at Jones (Miss.) CC, he struggled as a full-time pitcher at Alabama before thriving as a starter on a Jacksonville State team that won a school-record 47 games. He compiled a 3.66 ERA with 78 strikeouts in 66 1/3 innings and is one of the best college senior prospects available.

Scouts have been trying to figure out Vigue since his days as Massachusetts high schooler, when he could be unhittable at times and unable to find the strike zone others. That pattern continued in two years at Michigan, where he went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible in 2025. After switching schools, he has had an up-and-down season as Georgia's No. 2 starter and missed a turn in the rotation in late April with forearm tightness. Vigue gets more horizontal separation between his fastball and slider than almost any pitcher in the college crop. His 93-95 mph sinker reaches 98 with significant armside run, while his mid-80s slider has huge sweep in the opposite direction. He has utilized those two offerings 95 percent of the time this spring, rarely using a low-90s cutter and upper-80s changeup. Vigue generates plenty of swings and misses with his slider and weak contact with his fastball, but he has great difficulty landing either pitch in the zone on a regular basis. He rarely works past five innings, running up high pitch counts when hitters lay off his slider or he can't command his sinker. He has a strong 6-foot-3, 230-pound frame and a delivery that should provide more strikes, giving hope that he can add a third pitch and succeed as a starter in pro ball, but realistically he's more of a reliever.

Keenan was a solid Northern California high school prospect but was intent on heading to Stanford, where he’s pitched as a reliever and starter, albeit inconsistently and sporadically. There was some buzz about him getting a chance to start this year, but an oblique injury shelved him for half of the season. He’s up to 99 mph with his fastball with a short and clean delivery while showing an average sweeper, fringy cutter and developing changeup. He might be better off in a multi-inning relief role as he tended to lose steam, and command, past his second or third inning.

Johnson spent his first two college seasons at Dallas Baptist and McLennan (Texas) CC, winning Most Outstanding Defensive Player honors at the 2025 Junior College World Series. He's athletic and features plus arm strength to go with solid raw power, but he has yet to fully tap into the latter. He batted .330/.432/.538 with nine homers in 54 games as a junior.

Sims has the most electric arm in the high school class and repeatedly pushed his fastball to 100 mph on the showcase circuit last summer. He also has a 6-foot-8, 215-pound frame with plenty of room to add strength, so there may be more velocity to come. After winning an Oklahoma state 6-A championship at Edmond Santa Fe HS last spring, he transferred to Prestonwood Christian Academy (Plano, Texas) and won a Texas Association of Private and Parochial Schools Division I title. Sims previously worked from a three-quarters arm angle and topped out at 97 mph with more sink on his four-seamer. After raising his slot in the past year, he now operates at 94-97 and reaches triple digits with more carry. He generates outstanding velocity with arm speed and little effort, another reason to project future velocity gains. The rest of his arsenal needs work, because he lacks consistency with his shapes and control with his mid-80s slider and changeup. Sims still is learning to keep his extra-long limbs in sync in his delivery, and while he throws his heater for strikes, his fastball command is a work in progress. He'll require time to develop and comes with reliever risk but also immense arm talent. He'll turn 19 a month before the 2026 Draft and would be sophomore-eligible in 2028 if he follows through on his Oklahoma commitment.

Tiroly spent his first two years of college ball at Rider University in New Jersey, earning Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors as a sophomore. He entered the transfer portal and landed at Virginia, but a foot injury suffered at the end of the fall kept him from showing the Cavaliers or scouts checking him out in his new environment for the first time what he could do. A lack of prep time because of the injury, as well as not being 100 percent to start the spring led to a very slow start, but he was growing on evaluators as he heated up in ACC play. After having so much success in the MAAC, it was unclear how Tiroly would perform against a higher level of competition in a top conference. The right-handed hitter literally couldn't put his best foot forward, not facing live pitching until opening weekend and wearing a boot between games. As he put the injury behind him, he started showing off a much better feel to hit, with more pop in conference play, answering that question about his ability to handle ACC pitching. Tiroly wasn't a runner before the injury, so that part of his game wasn't impacted in any real way. He's a capable defender at both second and third, with enough arm for the hot corner. Some feel that might be his better position because of a lack of overall range, though playing third would put more pressure on him to keep showing an impact bat at the plate.

Ballinger was one of the most devastating junior college hitters in the country at the CC of Southern Nevada in 2024, then encored with one of the best offensive performances in Kansas history last year. But he slumped to .283/.401/.466 with seven homers in 60 games this spring as his timing got out of whack and he couldn't get to his plus raw power. All of his value comes from his bat, so he'll have to up his production in pro ball.

Tryba served as one of Santa Barbara’s key relievers for three years, racking up 13 saves and a 12.4 K/9 rate in his career, while also pitching effectively in the Cape Cod League in 2025. The lefty throws his 90-92 mph fastball, upper-70s sweeping slider, a mid-80s cutter and low-80s changeup from a funky lower slot that adds deception. It’s a relief-only profile, but he does tend to be around the plate.

Though he's a 6-foot right-hander who averages 92 mph with his fastball, Harpster should become the third-highest drafted pitcher ever out of East Tennessee State. He won't go as high as 1979 first-rounder Atlee Hammaker or 2020 second-rounder Landon Knack, but his metrics and ability to miss bats with his fastball and cutter are attractive to teams. A fixture in the Buccaneers rotation since early in his freshman season, he generated some of the best fastball and breaking ball spin rates at the MLB Draft Combine. Harpster's heater tops out at 95 mph but plays well above its velocity thanks to its flat approach angle and carry. His mid-80s cutter works better than its radar-gun readings as well because he excels at locating it where hitters will chase it but will be unable to barrel it. He also can shape a low-80s slider with more sweeping action, while his upper-80s changeup features some fade and sink but lags behind the rest of his repertoire. Harpster slings the ball and creates premium deception with an extremely low release point and good extension in his delivery. While his walk rate jumped from 6 percent as a sophomore to 11 percent this spring, he still showed advanced feel for working on the edges of the strike zone. If a pro team can help him add some velocity, he'll become even more intriguing.

Rhudy throws a lot of fastballs and he throws a lot of strikes. That approach worked for two seasons at Kennesaw State and continued to bring him success in the Southeastern Conference, college baseball's best league, after he transferred to Tennessee for his junior season.
