He compiled a 3.38 ERA and 41/6 K/BB ratio in 32 innings while ranking among the NCAA Division I leaders in fastball rates of chases (41 percent), swings and misses (35 percent) and in-zone swings and misses (28 percent). Rhudy's heater sits at 91-93 mph and reaches 96, but hitters can't lay off it or catch up to it despite its below-average velocity. His fastball is special because he creates huge spin rates and significant carry coming from a low release height and flat approach angle. He utilizes it about 70 percent of the time while employing a tight upper-70s slider to throw off batters' timing. The extension in Rhudy's low-three-quarters delivery adds to his deception. He pounds the strike zone and ranked third in D-I in overall (72 percent) and fastball (77 percent) strike percentage. He's purely a reliever but his unhittable heater might make him a high-leverage option, especially if a pro team can help him gain more velocity.

Barrett confounded hitters with his 90-96 mph fastball and 82-85 mph changeup, in part because he creates plenty of extension in his delivery. He compiled a 2.58 ERA, .194 opponent and 64/15 K/BB ratio in 45 innings. He had Tommy John surgery in 2024 while at UC Santa Barbara and missed time with elbow tightness this spring.

A Wisconsin high school product, Burns began his college career by headlining Arizona State's rotation before shoulder tendinitis ended his freshman season after six starts. He has operated out of Texas' bullpen the last two years, impressing with his fastball but never throwing enough strikes to lock down the closer's role. He recorded a 5.64 ERA this season despite striking out 42 percent of the batters he faced. Burns parks at 95-98 mph and peaks at 100 with a fastball that plays even better than its velocity because of the riding action he creates coming out of a nearly over-the-top arm slot. His upper-80s cutter can be a plus pitch when it's on, but he almost never lands it for strikes, and it remains to be seen how effective it will be against pro hitters. His mid-80s changeup lacks life and often misses the zone so badly that it elicits few chases. The effort in Burns' delivery has resulted in a 16 percent walk rate in three college seasons. Though he's one of the more intriguing pure relievers in the Draft and possesses an explosive fastball, it will be hard to trust him in high-leverage situations unless he improves his well-below-average control and command. Few college pitchers can match his ability to get in-zone swings and misses with three different pitches, but he has so much difficulty finding the zone.

Wright starred in two seasons at Bowling Green State, winning Mid-American Conference Freshman of the Year honors in 2024 and Defensive Player of the Year accolades in 2025. He also led the MAC with a .503 on-base percentage in his first season and with a .406 batting average and .513 OBP before transferring to Tennessee. Though a broken hamate in his left hand required surgery and cost him the first three weeks of the season, he has been the Volunteers' best hitter this season and is one of the more athletic catchers available. Wright combines bat-to-ball skills with an extremely aggressive approach, chasing a ton of pitches yet making a lot of line-drive contact and rarely missing fastballs. The right-handed hitter slugged just .243 with wood bats in the Cape Cod League last summer and doesn't do a lot of damage against premium velocity, so he may not have more than 10-15 homer power. While his swing-at-everything mindset cuts into his walk totals, he enhances his on-base ability by getting hit by an excessive amount of pitches. Unlike most catchers, Wright can flash plus speed and is capable of playing center field. He has spent more time in center than behind the plate this year while recovering from his hamate injury but offers more value as a backstop. He's an effective receiver and blocker with solid arm strength.

High school players in the northeast are often late risers simply because it takes a while for the weather to warm up and for them to get going. Add in a winter sport like basketball to delay being seen as another reason for a player to be a bit of a pop-up guy. And when that player didn't play on the summer showcase circuit, they can really seem like they come out of nowhere. Plunkett checks off all three boxes, but the New York prepster's name was coming up more frequently in scout chatter as the season moved closer to the Draft. An athletic 6-foot-3, Plunkett certainly looks the part. The right-handed hitter has a smooth swing that is currently line-drive oriented, but it's easy to project plenty more raw power to come because his frame should be able to add plenty of strength as he matures. He'll show it off in batting practice at times, but there's not that much impact in games to date. Plunkett's athleticism also helps him defensively. He looks like he could stick at shortstop for a while, with enough arm and more to come, good actions and solid instincts. He might look like a collection of 50 grades, but that's a solid big leaguer, and there could be a lot more in the tank. He's committed to Binghamton for college, but there's been some buzz that he could be like a Matthew Ferrara type, who was an over-slot ninth-round signing by the Phillies in 2025, or even Michael Oliveto, a surprise supplemental first-round pick by the Tigers last year.

Some scouts believe Long is the best sleeper pitching prospect in Georgia's prep class. He has added velocity this spring to go with a projectable 6-foot-2 frame and feel for a three-pitch arsenal. He could go as high as the late third round if that would be enough to sign him away from Kennesaw State. After sitting at 90 mph and peaking at 93 with his fastball last summer, Long now operates at 92 and touches 95, though his heater could use more life. His slider has gained some power as well, parking around 80 mph and displaying promising spin even if it lacks consistency. His best present pitch is a fading low-80s changeup that's more advanced than most high school cambios. Long's athleticism, clean operation and loose arm bode well for his future control and command. He has the potential for three solid or better offerings with strike-throwing to match once he gets stronger and adds more polish. One of the younger mound prospects in the Draft, he didn't turn 18 until May.

Koenig transferred from North Dakota State and became part of a deep Mississippi pitching staff that fueled a run to the College World Series. Physically imposing at 6-foot-6 and 245 pounds, he owns a 94-98 mph fastball and an upper-80s slider, and he'll also break out an upper-80s splitter on occasion. He's also raw and his heater gets whacked because it lacks command and life, which led to a 6.35 ERA and .347 opponent average, albeit with a 33/7 K/BB ratio in 22 2/3 innings.

Scott projected as a possible top-two-rounds selection at Stanford in 2025 before his stuff and strikes regressed significantly. Georgia straightened him out in a piggyback role this spring, when he went 7-0 with five saves, a 4.22 ERA and 76 strikeouts in 59 2/3 innings. He's mainly a two-pitch guy, pairing a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 97 with ride and run with a mid-80s cutter.

While it can be challenging to see and evaluate players from eastern Canada, Omidi has been a bit of a fixture in showcases, from things like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Area Code Games to playing the last two years for the Canadian Junior National Team against professional competition in Minor League Spring Training and in the Dominican Republic. Hailing from the same Ontario high school that produced one-time big leaguer Jordan Balazovic, Omidi has shown some potential, particularly with the bat, while also raising some overall questions about his profile. With a boxy, 6-foot-1 build, Omidi has shown off some strength from the left side of the plate. There have been times where excellent contact skills have been on display, but some swing-and-miss concerns did pop up against some of the better Minor League arms he faced with Team Canada. There is definite raw pop for him to tap into, with strong hands and wrists, and he'll show off lofty power in batting practice. Omidi is an average runner, though speed isn't a big part of his game, and he has an average arm, but where he fits defensively long-term is an unanswered question. It's unlikely he'll be a shortstop at the next level, lacking the quick first step or range to play there, with some scouts thinking he can handle second and others believing third, which he's played a lot more of lately, is his best chance to stay on the dirt, with a corner outfield spot a possibility if the infield isn't working. Omidi loves to hit, and it will be his bat that teams will be interested in signing away from his commitment to Kentucky.

The son of five-time World Series champion Andy Pettitte, Luke was a prospect as right-handed pitcher with a quality mid-80s slider and a low-90s fastball. He injured his elbow as a sophomore in 2025, leading to Tommy John surgery that kept him off the mound this spring. Dallas Baptist gave him at-bats as a DH and he responded by slashing .337/.403/.693 with 16 homers in 42 games.

Dugger grew up around the game, with his father, Keith, having served as the long-time head trainer for the Rockies. The Colorado Player of the Year for his level, Dugger went on to UCLA and got considerable playing time as a freshman, then settled in as the Bruins' starting catcher as a sophomore in 2025. He was a stalwart behind the plate again this season, earning Second-team All-Big 10 honors, while being named a Buster Posey Award semifinalist for the No. 1 team in the country. A big, strong 6-foot-3 backstop who hits left-handed, Dugger checks off some boxes teams like. He makes a lot of contact, sees pitches and draws a lot of walks. Though he's more a manager of at-bats than a dangerous hitter right now, he has shown glimpses of being able to tap into his raw power, and there's some belief there will be more to come. He runs and moves well for a catcher. What will get Dugger drafted, and potentially to the big leagues, is his work behind the dish. He's an outstanding defender who is agile behind the plate, blocks and receives well, and his plus arm will help control the running game. His defense gives him a very high floor as a future Major League backup, but there might be some upside to tap into offensively for a guy who will still be only 20 at Draft time and who gets very high marks for his makeup.

The nephew of former Georgia basketball star and WNBA player Angel Robinson, Phelps starred as a freshman for the Bulldogs and with the U.S. collegiate national team in 2024. That put him in position to become a first-rounder as a 2025, but a rough sophomore season killed his chances before he withdrew from the Draft in mid-July. He has rebounded this spring, helping Georgia win the Southeastern Conference regular-season and tournament titles and hitting his way back into the top three rounds. Phelps generates tremendous bat speed from the right side of the plate, showing the ability to catch up to high-end velocity and produce impressive exit velocities. He has done a better job of staying under control at the plate in 2026, though he still chases too many pitches and is vulnerable to sliders. He has the tools to become a solid hitter with 25-homer power and enhances his on-base ability by getting hit by pitches (35 this spring, two shy of the NCAA Division I record). Phelps posts fringy run times out of the batter's box but can flash solid speed on occasion. The biggest question facing him is where he'll play in pro ball after trying all four corners as well as second base with the Bulldogs. He has spent the most time at third base but he lacks infield actions and possesses just average arm strength, making the hot corner a tough fit at the next level. Left field may be his best-case scenario and he could wind up at first base.

From the minute he arrived on campus, Hansen has been a member of the UC Irvine weekend rotation, making 16 starts as a freshman and 16 more as a sophomore in 2025 en route to earning First-Team All Big West honors. He was the Anteaters' Friday night starter once again this season, with mixed results, but his consistency and durability have him in position to join Andre Pallante (2019 fourth round) and Riley Kelly (2025 fourth round) as Irvine pitchers taken recently in the top several rounds. With a strong 6-foot-2 frame, there's nothing glamorous about how Hansen gets things done on the mound, but he has a legitimate three-pitch mix with an idea of how to use it and the ability to routinely go deep into starts. His fastball is generally in the 90-95 mph range, though he was showing a tick more velocity this year sitting 93-94. He commands it well and has shown he can get to more later in games, giving some hope there could be more consistent mph to come. He has an above-average 81-84 mph curve, and his 84-85 mph changeup flashes plus; combined, the two secondary offerings missed bats at a 39-percent clip in 2026. Hansen is around the zone with all of his offerings, but while his compact arm action adds deception, hiding the ball well, some scouts don't love his below-average extension. There is strong consensus that he has plus makeup and a nasty competitive streak, which could give him the chance to start long-term, albeit with a more limited ceiling.

Johnson's athleticism and potential to play shortstop could make him the first player drafted from Oklahoma's national championship team. A transfer from Wichita State, he's one of the few Sooners whose performance didn't drop precipitously in Southeastern Conference action. He's one of the twitchiest and fastest players in the college ranks. Johnson displays good feel for the barrel from the left side of the plate but chases too many non-fastballs out of the zone. He doesn't miss strikes and employs a line-drive approach. He has average raw power and is driving the ball more than ever, but he hasn't shown much pop with wood bats in summer leagues and may top out at 10-12 homers per season. A consistent plus-plus runner, Johnson can get from home to first in less than four seconds at his best and is an accomplished basestealer. He shows average arm strength at third base, where his fluid actions lead to the belief that he could handle shortstop in pro ball after seeing occasional action there for the Shockers. He also could become a dynamic center fielder or valuable super utilityman.

Tayman was named co-Big West Player of the Year in 2026 after hitting .357/.447/.672 with 18 homers and 57 RBIs, and he was named the Most Outstanding Player in the Los Angeles Regional to help the Mustangs move on to Super Regional play. He can punish fastballs and recognizes spin decently, showing the ability to loft the baseball, especially to his pull side. He does struggle against offspeed stuff and is prone to chase, while the jury is still out whether he can catch long-term.

Shelar is the latest prospect out of a Marist School (Atlanta) program that has produced seven big leaguers, most notably Kyle Farmer, and won 14 Georgia state championships. He's a physical player with an interesting combination of raw power and solid speed, and a team that believes in his bat could pay him a seven-figure bonus. If that doesn't happen, he'll head to Mississippi State. Already 6-foot-2 and 205 pounds, Shelar projects to have well-above-average raw power thanks to his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage. He led all high schoolers with 19 homers in 33 games this spring. There are mixed opinions about his bat, with some scouts worrying about his ability to make consistent contact against pro pitching. He takes aggressive hacks with an unorthodox right-handed stroke that can get uphill. If he does hit enough to tap into his pop, Shelar has the solid speed to become at least a 20-20 player. A center fielder in high school, he doesn't have a quick first step but covers ground once he gets going. He likely will wind up on a corner in the long run and has the arm strength and offensive profile to fit in right field.

The top starter on a Georgia Tech team that ranked No. 2 in the nation for much of the season, McKee backs up a fastball that sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with a hard slider in the mid-80s. He's the only NCAA Division I hurler to start every series opener for his team through the past two seasons. He logged a 4.15 ERA with 99 strikeouts in 78 innings this spring.

Bonn spent two years at Pepperdine and one at Dallas Baptist before settling in as Cal Poly’s closer as a senior. The 6-foot 1 right-hander is a plus athlete whose 17 saves led all Division I pitchers, and he got it done with a fastball that sits around 95 mph but has touched triple digits while flashing a plus splitter and sweeper.

Because the Iowa high school season runs deep into July, LaFavor didn't get seen on the showcase circuit last summer. He has intrigued some evaluators this spring with his ultraprojectable 6-foot-7 frame and delivery metrics, and he'll get scouted more heavily in June and July. There are some parallels to Jacob Misiorowski at the same stage of their Midwest prep careers, though no one is predicting that LaFavor will explode to that extent. LaFavor's fastball can touch 95 mph early in games before settling in at 90-93 with some armside run and carry. His low-80s slider features sweeper action, and he also will turn it into an upper-80s cutter at times. He shows some aptitude for killing spin on an upper-70s changeup with fade. LaFavor's size and ability to get down the mound creates 7 feet plus of extension in his delivery, while his low arm slot produces wide angle and a low release height. Though the Iowa recruit's mechanics create deception, some scouts have concerns about his long arm action, effort and crossfire. He's still growing into his body and needs more strength so he can do a better job of repeating his delivery and locating his pitches, though he's more polished than Misiorowski was as a high school senior.

Alwood was born in Japan and went to high school in Hawaii before heading to Seattle University for college ball. The 6-foot-5 right-hander has had some opportunities to start for the Redhawks and could have a chance to do so at the next level even though he mostly relieved as a senior in 2026. He has a four-pitch mix with a fastball that sat 93 mph and topped out at 98 this season. His low-80s slider is his go-to, but his full array of secondaries (slider, curve, changeup) combined to miss bats at a 53-percent rate in '26 and his increasing confidence in his improved delivery could give him a shot at a rotation to start out his pro career.

Moroney has been a regular presence as Rhode Island’s shortstop for the past three years and is coming off his best offensive season, earning Second Team All-Atlantic 10 honors after hitting .370/.426/.494. He makes a ton of contact, limiting swing-and-miss, but does so with little impact. He was named the A10 Defensive Player of the Year and is a steady defender, though while scouts think he can start out at the premium position, he might end up at second base.

The best player to ever come out of Butler Area High School north of Pittsburgh is right-hander Matt Clement, a 1993 third-rounder who spent parts of nine years in the big leagues, but there hasn't been a player drafted from the program since 2003. This year, the Golden Tornado have a pair of right-handed pitchers who have intrigued scouts. The scouting industry might have had Nolan Stefaniak ahead of Casteel entering the spring, but that's likely flipped as the latter has made some big strides this spring. Casteel's combination of size, projection and improved pitchability had teams running to western Pennsylvania to get more looks at him.The 6-foot-4 hurler typically sits around 92 mph and tops out at 95 mph, but he can maintain the low-90s velocity deep into starts, and it's easy to dream about more to come as he fills out his frame. He has a slider that has the chance to be a true out pitch, mostly with three-quarters shape, depth and bite, though he can manipulate it into more of a slurve or a sweeper as he needs it. He doesn't use his changeup much, but it has the chance to be a solid third offering with some fade. In addition to Casteel's stuff ticking up, he also showed a better feel for finding the zone, with solid command and control compared to looks from the fall. The feel for pitching and pure arm strength point to some ceiling here, with some evaluators talking about the West Virginia recruit in the top five rounds.

TNXL Academy in Florida has a trio of Draft prospects who could all go in the top several rounds. Genson Veras is the bat scouts like, while evaluators can pick between a pair of different arms in Coleton Brady and Spencer Evans. While Brady's feel for pitching is better, Evans has showcased better pure stuff from the left side, starting at summer showcase events like East Coast Pro Showcase and USA Baseball's 18U National Team Camp and continuing into this year, albeit with less strikes overall. Evans offers a combination of size (6-foot-3), projection and arm strength. Combine that with the fact that he's left-handed, and that's sure to intrigue teams. At times, he can look like a first-round caliber talent, with a fastball routinely up to 95-96 mph and flashing two above-average secondary offerings. He's added velocity to what is now a low-80s slider and can miss a lot of bats with it, throwing the breaker with good angles. His mid-80s changeup continues to improve. As good as that package sounds, Evans is often stuff over performance, with his command and control the biggest culprit in keeping him ineffective. He's prone to walks and comes with a little left-handed reliever risk, but he's athletic and moves easily on the mound. A team that sees enough future starter in him could try to sign him away from his commitment to Louisiana State.

Norman owns a 93-95 mph fastball that climbs to 97 along with a mid-80s slider and upper-80s cutter. He provides plenty of strikes and creates good extension in his delivery, but his stuff gets hit harder than it should. He logged a 6.46 ERA with 65 strikeouts in 78 innings during his first year at Coastal Carolina after two at Georgia State.

Williams is a target for teams looking for athletes in the middle rounds. He's a 6-foot-2, 195-pounder with well above-average speed and some power potential, though he still needs polish at the plate and in center field. He slashed .343/.458/.545 with 10 homers and 32 steals in 60 games.

Every year there are players who take a large step forward in their Draft season, pop-up prospects as they're generally known. Barker has been one of those players in the Four Corners. After not being seen much on the summer showcase circuit, Barker started showing off his raw tools as his Casteel High School made it to USA Baseball's National High School Invitational semifinals, and that continued this spring as Casteel advanced to the second round of the Arizona state playoffs. Barker is a super-athletic left-handed hitter who plays the infield in high school. Everything about him is a little raw, but there are glimpses of him doing everything well. It's a hit-over-power approach, and those who like him see an average hit tool in there, though he'll have to continue to add strength to his 6-foot-1 frame to get to more impact, even if he's never a huge power guy. The one purely plus tool he has is his speed, and some scouts have seen 70-grade run times from him occasionally. Where Barker best profiles defensively is also a question. He has some abilities to play short but had been seeing most of his time on the dirt at third base this spring. His bat might not profile well for the corner infield spot, and his overall defense needs work, with some thinking he might fit in a 3B/2B/LF kind of role. Those who like him are all about projection, but some think he'd be better off going to Texas Tech, where he'd be a Draft-eligible sophomore in two years.

While Georges has long had size and arm strength, his path to being a high-level Draft prospect was anything but certain. As a sophomore at Clovis High School outside of Fresno, California, Georges blew out his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. He returned to the mound in time for league play as a junior in 2025, then put the injury further in his rearview by throwing at a myriad of summer showcase events, including Major League Baseball's All-American Game, Perfect Game National and the Area Code Games. While Georges' senior year has had some ups and downs, he still brings an ideal 6-foot-5 pitching frame to the mound with the chance to have a quality three-pitch mix with excellent metrics under the surface. He'll throw his fastball in the 92-96 mph range; it can have carry and ride, and he also has a two-seamer with good sink. He'll flash a plus low-80s slider that can miss bats, giving him an effective sinker-sweeper combination at times. He's shown glimpses of a very solid 84-85 mph changeup with sink and fade he'll throw to hitters on both sides of the plate. Georges hasn't always thrown quality strikes this spring, and at times, things can snowball for him on the mound. He'll also be 19 come Draft time, which might ding him in some teams' models. Even so, his stuff and the data behind it could be enough to get teams interested in signing him away from his commitment to Texas Christian.

Haley never pitched much because of an assortment of injuries that extends from a torn elbow ligament that required Tommy John surgery when he was a high school junior to forearm tightness this spring. A former two-way player who saw infield action as a freshman in 2024, he owns a 93-95 mph fastball that hits 97 and a pair of hard breaking pitches in an 85-88 mph slider/cutter and an 82-84 mph curveball. He posted a 3.07 ERA with 20 strikeouts in 14 2/3 innings in 2026.

An older prospect, at 22, who came to junior college ball from Switzerland, Bundi led all California JUCO pitchers in strikeouts in 2026. The athletic 6-foot-2 right-hander has a starter’s delivery with good command of a four-pitch mix: a fastball he throws in the 90-95 mph range, a power 79-82 mph curve that flashes plus, an average changeup with depth and a cutter. He’s committed to UCLA next year if he doesn’t enter pro ball.

After spending the 2025 season pitching in Santa Barbara’s rotation, there was excitement about what Proskey might be able to do behind Jackson Flora as a junior. He missed the first half of the season with a UCL strain but was effective over eight starts upon his return, then showed off his four-pitch mix at the MLB Draft Combine. His fastball sits only around 91 mph, but he has good feel to spin a 78-80 mph 12-to-6 curve and a less effective low-80s slider, while showing he can kill spin on his 84-85 mph changeup.

McHugh makes consistent contact and is more athletic than the typical first baseman, though scouts would like to see him generate more power by lifting more pitches. He batted .320/.409/.525 with nine homers in 56 games this spring and has totaled 22 blasts between two seasons with the Wolfpack and one at Virginia Commonwealth.

A two-way player with some promise on the mound, Adams has cemented his future as a position player this spring. The consensus is that he owns one of the prettiest left-handed swings in the 2026 high school class, though there are some mixed opinions how much power he'll ultimately have. A club that believes he could get to 25 homers per season while remaining on an outfield corner could take him as early as the second round. Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year, Adams employs a patient approach and has a history of making consistent contact to all fields. In the past, he would get too passive at times and didn't tap into his raw power on a regular basis. He's doing a better job of being selectively aggressive and turning his quick stroke loose as a senior, enabling him to drive balls in the air to his pull side more often. While Adams can display average speed at times, he figures to be no better than a fringy runner once he's physically mature. The Louisiana State recruit has decent range but is still refining his reads and routes as a right fielder, while some scouts believing he's destined to wind up at first base, where he's a solid defender. His arm isn't a question because he reaches 91 mph with his fastball while showing feel for an upper-70s changeup and slider.

Queen spent a year starting at Everett Community College before becoming an effective reliever at Oregon State in 2025 and '26. He finished with a 2.49 ERA in '26 to go along with a .205 BAA and 14.9 K/9 rate. The 6-foot-2 right-hander relies heavily on his mid-80s slider, which produced a 62 percent miss rate this season. His fastball is typically in the 92-94 mph range, he’ll mix in an effective slower curve, and a changeup is his fourth offering. His arsenal and his tendency to be around the zone could give him a chance to start as a pro.

Model-based teams might really have an interest in Martin, who is still only 20 years old after three years of making a ton of contact at the University of Maryland. He led the Terps in hitting (.352), OBP (.488) and steals (21), among several offensive categories, in 2026. He struck out less than 10 percent of the time in his career, albeit without much impact, and drew a ton of walks. He’s played all over defensively, with second base perhaps being his best chance at a regular home.

Though Holcomb was an all-state tight end at Foundation Academy (Winter Garden, Fla.), he preferred to use his physicality on the diamond. He spurned interest from pro teams out of high school to attend Vanderbilt, and he was the Commodores' best hitter (.352/.434/.621) this spring. There aren't many college players who can match his size (6-foot-5, 245 pounds) or history of playing five different positions. Holcomb's strength gives him well-above-average raw power, and he can drive the ball out of the park to all fields from the right side of the plate. But he doesn't maximize his pop because he's way too aggressive, chasing all types of pitches, struggling to make contact on offerings on and off the plate and not catching up to quality velocity. He has 30-homer ceiling but has slugged just .388 with wood bats in two seasons in the Cape Cod League and might not make enough contact to do damage in the Majors. Holcomb has sneaky athleticism with average speed, and he'll flash solid run times and steal bases on occasion. He covers enough ground to get the job done on the outfield corners and played a surprisingly adequate center field when he saw action there this spring. He has the solid arm strength for third base but is a stiff defender there, while first base is a viable option.

After a solid high school career at California powerhouse Huntington Beach, Aceves headed to UC Santa Barbara, where he pitched effectively in relief as a freshman, earning NCBWA Freshman All-America Second Team honors in the process. In 2026, scouts could come watch the Gauchos back-to-back, getting first-round prospect Jackson Flora on Fridays and Aceves following him the next day. Aceves wasn't as dominant as his rotation-mate, though the All-Big West Honorable Mention starter did win an essential elimination game to propel Santa Barbara to an NCAA Regional final. Scouts who like Aceves point to his combination of size at 6-foot-3 and arm strength. The right-hander pitches with a fastball that sits around 93-95 mph, but he can reach back for 96-97 on occasion. His best pitch is his plus changeup, thrown around 85 mph, that can fall off the table with serious fade. He can get to an average upper-70s curve and he has an upper-80s slider he throws less frequently. While Aceves tends to generally be around the zone, his command is probably average at best. There's some concern with his delivery mechanics and less-than-clean arm stroke, with some inversion and unorthodox arm positions as a result. There's enough interest in the arm strength here to imagine Aceves will hear his name called at some point on Day 2.

Krodel spent the year pitching out of Santa Barbara’s bullpen, but there are some who think the 6-foot-4 projectable right-hander could have a chance to start as a pro. He’ll show flashes of four above-average pitch shapes, starting with a fastball that sits 90-93 and tops out at 95. He’ll show a plus low-80s changeup that elicited a 46 percent miss rate in 2026 and a plus sweeper that also misses bats (54 percent) while also showing feel for an average upper-70s curve. He has good extension and if he can refine his command, he could stick in a rotation.

Ranked No. 230 on MLB Pipeline's 2025 Draft Top 250, Arvidson redshirted at Texas A&M and starred at San Jacinto (Texas) JC before spending the last two years at Tennessee. He relies heavily on a low-80s slider, setting it up with a low-90s fastball that climbs as high as 95 mph with some carry but not much life. He compiled a 4.34 ERA with 44 strikeouts in 37 1/3 innings as a reliever and could get a chance to start in pro ball.

Fitzwater leaves VMI as the school’s career leader in a host of categories, including home runs (62), total bases (483) and RBIs (223). He set a single-season record with 21 homers as a senior in 2026. He has big-time raw power from the left side of the plate that he can get to thanks to good swing decisions, which helps him profile at first base or an outfield corner.

After slashing .353/.438 /.476 in his one season at Santa Ana Junior college, Long moved on to the University of Utah and spent two years as the Utes’ starting left fielder. He earned All-Big 12 Second Team honors in 2026 after hitting .374 with a 1.010 OPS. He’s a left-handed hitter with excellent contact skills to go along with some strength, power and metrics that analytics departments will like.

Thomas didn’t get regular playing time over two years at Cal so he transferred to Cal State Northridge for his junior season, with solid results. He led the Big West in slugging percentage (.679) and was second in OPS (1.090), earning First Team All-Big West honors in the process. Young for the class at age 20, he’s a solid athlete with a power-over-hit profile, with enough bat speed to give some confidence he can keep getting to his plus raw power. He’s a solid athlete who should be able to handle an outfield corner well.

A pitchability southpaw, Fisher pounds the zone with a low-90s fastball to set up his best pitch, an upper-70s curveball. He compiled a 5.59 ERA with a 58/17 K/BB ratio in 56 innings this spring, enjoying early-season success but struggling in Southeastern Conference play.

When most baseball fans think about Notre Dame High School talent in recent years, Hunter Greene (2017) comes to mind, with Giancarlo Stanton ten years earlier. The program hasn't had a position player taken in the top 10 rounds since 2009, but Madrid hopes to buck that trend this July. The catcher wasn't seen all that much on the summer showcase circuit but was impressing both area scouts and cross-checkers during his senior year, particularly with his work behind the dish. Madrid's calling card is his defense. His abilities behind the plate give him a very high floor, with some evaluators claiming he has the best arm of any young catcher they've seen this year. It's not just pure arm strength, as he also has a quick release and is very accurate controlling the running game. His overall defensive package, including receiving and blocking, is quite advanced. His ultimate ceiling will be determined by how much he hits. More than one scout gave a report that included a version of, if he hits at all, he's a big leaguer. The Oregon recruit does have some raw power that he's gotten to in games at times in front of evaluators, and a team that saw enough of that might look past the typically tough right-right high school catching profile to sign him away from his college commitment.

Beck wasn't a regular on the showcase circuit, so scouts flocked to Tennessee to check out his raw power this spring. It was apparent at the MLB Draft Combine, where he hit the longest drive (466 feet) on the second day or workouts and smoked 21 balls harder than 100 mph, with a peak of 113. He’ll play third base at the next level, either in pro ball or at Georgia Southern.

Carrier could be an interesting fifth-year senior sign. He has legitimate raw power that he got to enough to smash 20 homers and earn First-Team All-ACC honors in 2026. It comes with a good amount of swing-and-miss, though he did cut down his strikeout rate considerably this season. He has a strong arm that profiles well in right field.

A 6-foot-6 right-hander who spent three years at the University of Washington, racking up seven saves as a junior, Yeager was a valuable senior reliever at Oregon State this year. His low-80s slider produced a 55 percent miss rate this year, and he threw the pitch more than his low-90s riding fastball. The slider can back up at times, but it’s hard to argue with the success he had this year: 2.04 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, .184 BAA and 11.1 K/9 rate.

Kapa has seen just about every level of college pitching, going from Division III Alma College to Mott Community College to Eastern Michigan and then finally to Virginia as a graduate student. He served as the Cavaliers’ closer, saving 11 games and striking out 11.7 per nine, with a fastball that touched 98 mph and missed a lot of bats to go along with an 83-84 mph gyro slider and flashes of a solid splitter.

A two-time participant in the Appalachian League, Ladd returned from 2025 Tommy John surgery this year. He started to get to the mid 90s with his fastball, coming from an extra-large 6-foot-6 frame. He backs up the heater with a traditional low-80s slider and a solid shorter 84-85 mph cutter while mixing in the occasional fringy low-80s changeup.

Johnson flashed first-round talent as a Florida high schooler in 2023 before missing some time with elbow tendinitis, and he turned down lucrative offers from several clubs to attend Louisiana State. Severe control issues led to him working just nine innings for the Tigers as a freshman before transferring to Oklahoma, where he has continued to battle the strike zone the last two years. He displayed improved control at the start of this season but regressed once Southeastern Conference play began and barely pitched in the postseason as the Sooners won the College World Series. Johnson can overpower hitters with a fastball that parks at 95 mph and peaks at 99 with heavy sink, though he often yanks it off the plate. His upper-80s changeup can miss bats with its depth, but he has landed it in the zone only 15 percent of the time this spring. Nevertheless, he trusts his cambio more than a low-80 slider with sweep that he barely uses and batters rarely offer at. With a wide angle, low release height and the extension in his delivery, Johnson can be very tough on left-handers. He has yet to figure out how to maintain timing with his mechanics or to stay on top of his pitches on a regular basis. He's a physical 6-foot-6, 256-pounder with a ceiling of a sinker-heavy starter, though evaluators are losing faith that he can reach it.

Harvard-Westlake High School in southern California has produced high-end Draft talent, from first-round quality arms like Lucas Giolito, Max Fried and Jack Flaherty to exciting hitters like Pete Crow-Armstrong and most recently, 2024 first-rounder Bryce Rainer. This year's entry is Tronstein, whose Draft stock was up in the air after he scuffled some on the summer showcase circuit but turned things around this spring, particularly in front of a lot of eyes at USA Baseball's National High School Invitational. An athletic 5-foot-11 right-handed bat, Tronstein is an aggressive hitter who is looking to do damage at all times. He's able to hit the ball very hard, like he did with some elite exit velocities at NHSI, and can drive the ball to all fields with some sneaky pop. He had a tendency to chase too much out of the zone over the summer, leading to some swing-and-miss concerns, and he has a penchant for lunging against soft stuff too much, something that will have to be addressed at the next level. Tronstein is an above-average runner, plus underway, and his speed can help him on both sides of the ball. He's played both shortstop and the outfield, and while he has an average arm, scouts tend to like him better in center, where his athleticism plays well, because his arm might be a bit shy for plays in the hole. The biggest hurdle for teams considering Tronstein might be his commitment to Vanderbilt.

All Garza has done in his three years at Cal Poly is hit, earning First Team All-Big West honors in all three seasons, with his .318 average in 2026 a career low that brought his Mustangs career mark down to .337. He’s an undersized (5-foot-9) infielder with very impressive bat-to-ball skills (5.4 career strikeout percentage), albeit without much impact, a sparkplug who plays above his tools.

Kucherak barely played at Louisiana State in 2024 before setting a Northwestern record with 18 homers last spring and going deep 10 times as a junior. He comes with some swing-and-miss concerns and struggled with wood bats in the Cape Cod League last summer, but he's also a middle infielder with solid raw power and speed.

A high school right-hander listed at 6-foot-2, Dunwoody offers plenty of arm strength to interested teams. He’s been up to 96 mph, though he pitched more in the 90-94 mph range during his senior season. He has an 82-85 mph slider, though it lacks real swing-and-miss action. The Arizona recruit is more thrower/arm strength than pitcher/polish at present.

Nasser is a tall and lanky left-handed-hitting outfielder with an outstanding approach and good bat-to-ball skills. There’s underlying power that could be unlocked with some swing adjustments at the next level. He’s an average runner whose excellent instincts give him the chance to play center field. Scouts really like the Oklahoma recruit’s baseball IQ and competitive streak.

In 2025, California prep power Corona High School saw three players get taken in the first 32 picks of the Draft. Murphy was arguably the best offensive performer on the team that saw right-hander Seth Hernandez and shortstop Billy Carlson go in the top 10 and Brady Ebel go No. 32 overall, with the outfielder hitting over .400 and slamming 11 homers as a junior. Murphy raised his profile at MLB Develops events like the Hank Aaron Invitational and Breakthrough Series, while shining at MLB's High School All-American Game and winning a gold medal with Team USA at the WSBC U-18 World Cup in Japan. A strong, physically mature right-handed-hitting outfielder, Murphy's two standout tools are his raw power and his defense. He has at least plus raw pop and has shown he can get to it in games in high school, but there are questions about his hit tool moving forward. He likes to change his swing and fiddle with his setup a lot, and there's been a good amount of swing-and-miss and chase as a result, though there's some conviction that finding consistency in his mechanics should allow him to find the barrel enough. A plus runner, Murphy is considered by some area scouts to be one of the best defensive outfielders they've seen in recent memory. He can play center field and if he slows down and moves to right, he has more than enough arm for the spot. All of the LSU recruit's tools play up because of his full-throttle, hard-nosed play, giving more confidence he'll maximize his ability as a pro.

Govel came for his official visit to Southern Cal four years ago and immediately formed a bond with Mason Edwards. It took a little time for that to translate to the field, especially since Govel redshirted his freshman year in 2024 following Tommy John surgery. But after scuffling through a 2025 season spent mostly in the Trojans' bullpen, he joined Edwards in the USC weekend rotation to form one of the best 1-2 punches in college baseball. Govel earned NCBWA Second-team All-American honors after finishing fourth among all Division I pitchers with an 0.90 WHIP and topping the Big 10 with his 6.19 K/BB ratio. A strong 6-foot, 200-pound right-hander, Govel might attack hitters with as many as six pitches. He has both a four-seam and newer two-seam fastball that typically sit around 91-92 mph, though he has topped out at 95. He has consistently shown consistent 94-95 mph heaters early in the spring, with 20-21 inches of induced vertical break on the four-seamer. His best secondary offering is a plus low-80s changeup he sells extremely well with arm speed that kills spin and has excellent depth at the plate, a cambio he'll throw to hitters on both sides. He has both a low-80s slider and an upper-70s bigger top-down curve, and a cutter that flashes average that he can get up to 90 mph. Govel delivers all of his offerings with a quick arm and a simple and repeatable stretch-only delivery. That leads to very good fastball command and excellent overall control that limits walks. His ceiling might be a bit limited, but his repertoire and feel to pitch could help him get to the big leagues as a back-end starter.

Transferring home to Western New York from Georgia Southern in 2025, Dalton Harper led the way to victory for the 2026 NJCAA Division III champs Niagara CCC Thunderwolves, winning national player of the year honors along the way. He hopes to follow his 2025 teammate Matt Barr in the professional ranks but will take his talents to Penn State if not selected this weekend.

One of the better sophomore-eligible prospects in the 2026 Draft, Wentz offers power from both sides of the plate and has helped his cause by improving his conditioning and athleticism. But he also has flummoxed scouts with his inability to stop chasing or do much damage against breaking balls and changeups. Viewed as a potential second-round choice entering 2026, he may have to wait a couple of more rounds to hear his name called. Wentz's combination of bat speed and strength gives him at least plus raw power, and he could tap into more of it if he became more selective and pulled more balls in the air. More effective from the left side, he destroys fastballs but scuffles against everything else, and his aggressiveness leaves him especially vulnerable to changeups. He draws his share of walks because pitchers are reticent to challenge him, but he needs to tone down his approach. The 6-foot-2, 215-pound Wentz is moving better as sophomore and displaying fringy speed. He has split his college career between third base and second base, and his limited range and solid arm strength fit better at the hot corner. He's an erratic defender at both positions, so he may wind up on an outfield corner.

Sutton barely pitched as a freshman at Georgia in 2024, then redshirted in 2025 as he rehabbed from Tommy John surgery. He moved to South Florida for '26 and settled in as the Bulls’ closer, saving nine games, striking out 10.5 per nine and holding hitters to a .223 batting average. His fastball sits around 93-94 mph and touches 97, and his low-80s changeup is his best secondary offering, though he does offer an 80-mph slurvy slider, all thrown with good extension.

The NCAA Division I batting champion with a .446 average, Mally also set Western Michigan records with 87 hits and a .554 on-base percentage. A career .400 hitter, he has elite bat-to-ball skills and well above-average speed that plays well on the bases and in center field, though he won’t provide much impact with wood bats.

The Florida panhandle is often a difficult area to get scouted due to its remote location. But evaluators will be spending plenty of time there just to see the pitching staff at South Walton High School. It's a group led by Coleman Borthwick, transfer Griffin Loy and Lord, a super-projectable right-hander whose size and stuff certainly garnered attention during the summer showcase circuit at events like the East Coast Professional Showcase and MLB's High School All-American Game. Lord is a tall and lanky 6-foot-8 right-hander with serious projection. His fastball will sit around 94 mph, though he's shown the ability to reach back for 97-98 mph in shorter stints, and he throws it with heavy sink. At times, he can really snap off a plus upper-70s curveball, though he can try to do too much with it and it becomes slurvy. He doesn't need a changeup in high school, but he did show a low-80s one occasionally over the summer, though it's more of a batting practice fastball than anything truly effective. All of Lord's arsenal comes from a fast, easy arm and it's easy to dream on more velocity to come as he fills out that frame and learns to sync up his delivery consistently, which should also help his command. He did have Tommy John surgery as a freshman but has shown no ill effects now. He switched his college commitment from Florida to Mississippi State and will play for Brian O'Connor should the Draft not go his way.

There is a constant desire for baseball to attract more athletes to the game, and the scouting industry has the chance to do just that with Bowen. The JSerra Catholic standout entered the summer as a former football player with raw tools and finished it rushing up Draft boards because of more confidence in his ability to use those tools with outstanding performances at showcase events like the Area Code Games. Bowen is a veritable toolshed in a strong, athletic 6-foot-3 package. A football standout who is now focusing on baseball only, he's a physical right-handed hitter who has always been able to punish the baseball. It might be 70-grade raw power, but the question in the past was if he would hit enough to get to it. There's been in-zone swing-and-miss in the past, but he found the barrel a lot more consistently over the summer, leading evaluators to be more bullish on his hitability. With plus athleticism that plays on the basepaths and in the outfield, Bowen has the chance to stick in center field, though he has the plus arm to profile well in right field if needed. He also gets high marks for his makeup and high energy play on the field. If the hit tool keeps improving, the Oregon State recruit could easily skyrocket into the first round.

Parkview HS (Lilburn, Ga.) is one of the most successful high school programs in the country, winning nine state titles and three national championships in the last three decades while producing talents such as Jeff Francoeur, Jeff Keppinger and Matt Olson. The latest Panthers prospect is Washington, who tied for ninth nationally with 15 homers in 37 games last spring. He has a track record of performing at showcase events but still comes with some questions about his bat. Washington is solidly built at 6-foot-1 and 203 pounds with strong hands and wrists. He has a quick right-handed swing and generates impressive exit velocities, but he also gets overly aggressive at the plate and can struggle against breaking balls. He shows the ability to drive the ball to all fields yet makes more groundball contact than is desired. Washington's speed and arm strength both earn solid to plus grades. The Louisiana State recruit has a good chance to remain in center field in college or pro ball, and his arm and power would fit the right-field profile if he has to shift to a corner. He earns praise for his work ethic as well as his tools.

Ponatoski won Gatorade's Ohio Player of the Year awards in both baseball and football as a junior in 2024-25, joining Joe Mauer and Randy Moss as the only athletes to earn Gatorade honors in two sports in the same academic year. A four-star quarterback recruit committed to Kentucky in both sports, he skipped summer football workouts with the Wildcats. He may not have pitched enough for his signability to align with his ability for most clubs. Ponatoski's most impressive pitching performance was a one-inning stint at the East Coast Pro showcase last August, when he operated at 93-95 mph with carry and armside run on his fastball and displayed a plus curveball with power and downer break in the low 80s. This spring, his heater often settled at 90-92 mph after an inning or two and his curve wasn't as sharp. His mid-80s changeup is too firm and very much a work in progress. While Ponatoski is athletic and provides strikes, he's not particularly projectable at 6-foot-2 and 200 pounds. He totaled about 30 innings between his junior and senior seasons, plus the showcase circuit, and he might take off if he focuses on pitching after preferring to play shortstop in the past. He's a long-term project with upside but won't realize it until he commits to baseball full-time.

Santarelli emerged as one of the best power hitters in the 2026 high school class while topping Wisconsin prepsters with 11 homers in 31 games as a junior (despite drawing 44 walks), leading St. Joseph (Kenosha) to the state Division 3 championship. He rose to the occasion on the showcase circuit as well, winning MVP honors at the MLB High School All-American Game, putting on a show during the Home Run Derby and during game action at the Under Armour Next All-America Game. Gatorade's 2026 Wisconsin high school player of the year, he has the ceiling of a more athletic version of Kyle Schwarber. Physically imposing at 6-foot-2 and 230 pounds, Santarelli has a relatively compact left-handed swing that unleashes high exit velocities and tape-measure shots to all fields. Though he knows his plus-plus raw power means he doesn't have to sell out to crush home runs and he has the discipline to take walks when pitchers decline to challenge him, he's a streaky hitter who can lapse into strikeouts. He's still working on pitch recognition and maintaining a consistent stroke. Faster than most players his size, Santarelli can flash solid straight-line speed and plays as a fringy runner. His defense needs a lot of work, because he's rough at first base and has below-average arm strength. The Louisiana State recruit has the work ethic to improve his glove and throwing and could merit a look in left field.

Though McCoy recorded a 7.11 ERA in his first two seasons at South Carolina, a brief but dominant stint in the Cape Cod League last summer left some evaluators wondering if he might be the best college left-hander in the 2026 Draft. He struck out 25 of the 54 Cape batters he faced while issuing just three walks in three starts. He has the stuff and metrics to back up that performance and will have to show that he can sustain it, but he won't get the chance to do so this year after blowing out his elbow in January and requiring Tommy John surgery. McCoy's fastball gained a couple of ticks of velocity on the Cape, parking at 94-95 mph and peaking at 98 with natural cutting action. He also threw a nasty mid-80s slider with plenty of sweep and mixed in some true cutters at 87-91 mph. He doesn't have much trust in a fading upper-80s changeup that he struggles to locate. McCoy's low three-quarters arm slot and resulting low release height create pitches with an unusual combination of velocity and shapes that are hard for hitters to deal with. He lacks size, has effort in his delivery and doesn't have much track record of success or strikes, so he might be more reliever than starter. He looked like he could pitch in the front half of a rotation while on the Cape, and he has the arsenal for a high-leverage role if he does wind up in the bullpen.

Moutzouridis spent his first two college seasons at California before transferring to Arizona State for his junior year. While his numbers were modest (.286/.410/.417 in 2026), he’s a college contact bat who knows how to see a lot of pitches and get on base, all while showing he can play shortstop at the next level.

Escalante’s premium athleticism stands out on the mound more than anything else. A wide receiver on his high school football team, he’s a left-hander with a fastball up to 93 mph, and he was showing more life with the pitch before he went down with an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. His feel to spin is behind the fastball, and the Cal State Fullerton recruit is a deep projection play, especially because whatever team takes him will have to rehab him post-surgery.

Freshcorn led the Southeastern Conference with 12 saves and posted a 2.27 ERA with a 51/5 K/BB ratio in 47 2/3 innings. He throws a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96, a mid-80s cutter and a low-80s slider, and his low release height and quality extension help his stuff play up.

Back trouble limited DeVaughan's exposure on the showcase circuit last summer, but he made up for lost time by reaching 96 mph with his fastball and 92 with his cutter at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October. He came out throwing even harder this spring while allowing no runs and just two hits while striking out 40 in his first 16 innings. He has emerged as one of the best high school pitching prospects in the Midwest and should become the first player ever drafted out of Mooresville (Ind.) HS, though he missed most of May while dealing with a scapular issue. With plenty of arm speed and little effort, DeVaughn produces four-seam fastballs that sit at 93-95 mph and top out at 98 with riding action, and he also owns an 89-91 mph two-seamer that sinks and a cutter with similar velocity. He shows feel for spinning a pair of breaking balls, a 78-80 mph curveball and an 82-84 mph slider with similar shape. He does a nice job of killing spin on a mid-80s changeup that fades, though he hasn't needed it much at this point. DeVaughan has a very projectable 6-foot-5 frame, so there should be more velocity to come. He has no problem throwing strikes while delivering pitches from a high three-quarters arm slot. If he follows through on his commitment to Alabama, he'll be Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2028.

While Fennell lacks physicality and overpowering stuff, he's a metrics darling with outlier low release height and extension that help his pitches play up. His fastball sits at 88 mph and maxes out at 91 but gets plenty of chases and swings and misses thanks to its shape and carry. His low-70s changeup has screwball action, though he lacks feel for spinning a breaking ball. It's unclear how his repertoire will fare in pro ball, though there are a number of teams willing to find out.

The Orioles took a 19th-round flier on Ritchie, a slugger from a small-town Oklahoma high school, in the 2023 Draft but couldn't dissuade him from attending Oklahoma State. Despite rarely facing fastballs harder than 80 mph as a prepster, he became an immediate starter for the Cowboys. He has improved his production each season and ranked fourth in NCAA Division I with 31 homers this spring. A left-handed hitter, Ritchie translates bat speed and strength into well-above-average raw power that plays from foul pole to foul pole. He maximizes it by looking to launch balls in the air to his pull side, though his overly aggressive approach leads to concerns about how much he'll hit in pro ball. He swings through too many strikes, chases soft stuff and has struggled to make contact with wood bats in the Cape Cod League. Ritchie moves well for a 6-foot-2, 228-pounder and shows solid speed once he gets going. He gets the job done in center field for Oklahoma State, though he profiles better on the corners at the next level. He has average arm strength and some experience playing third base as well.

A University of North Carolina recruit, Lawson is a 6-foot-2 right-hander with a maxed-out body and an average fastball that gets up to 94 mph. His bread and butter is his future plus curve that can miss bats. He gets high marks for his competitiveness on the mound and he also played first base and hit in the middle of his Bishop Verot lineup this year.
